## Overview

What is this document? This document is an attempt to formalize Marin’s policy towards what constitutes reportable, public-facing, canonical eval results for Marin models as well as the baselines we compare against.

Why do we need this document? With the first “snowball” release of a 67B A2B MoE, Marin is entering a regime where we regularly compare Marin models to existing open and closed-source models. Because Marin’s unique claim is that we are open development, we will need to hold ourselves to a high standard of transparency on how we report eval scores of Marin models and what claims we make about Marin model capabilities based on those scores.

What is in scope for this document? This document is intended to act as a living snapshot, trustworthy for any given period in time, as to the what and the how of Marin’s canonical set of evals, a set of standards to which we will aspire to hold ourselves. By "the what", we mean “which evals did we run, with what consistent set of hyperparameters and experimental constraints”. By "the how", we mean “where is the self-contained codebase that is both necessary and sufficient to reproduce our eval results independently”.

## Previous version notes

* Released Sept 16, 2026: 11 Evalchemy benchmarks, 8 lm-eval-harness tasks and 5 Harbor agentic evals in-distribution

## Complete eval list, with hyperparameters

### In Distribution

| Eval | Framework | Metric | Shots | Repetitions | Thinking mode | Allowed context length | Mean time-to-complete |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| MATH-500 | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item | on | 73,664 tokens | — |
| HumanEval+ | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item | off | 73,664 tokens | — |
| MBPP+ | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item | off | 73,664 tokens | — |
| OlympiadBench (30-question subset) | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 10 samples per item | on | 73,664 tokens | — |
| GSM8K | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item | off | 73,664 tokens | — |
| PIQA | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 choice decision per item | not applicable | 73,664 tokens | — |
| WinoGrande | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 5 | 1 run × 1 choice decision per item | not applicable | 73,664 tokens | — |
| BoolQ | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 choice decision per item | not applicable | 73,664 tokens | — |
| TruthfulQA | lm-eval-harness | mc2 | 0 | 1 run × 1 scored answer set per item | not applicable | 73,664 tokens | — |
| TriviaQA | lm-eval-harness | accuracy | 5 | 1 run × 1 sample per item | off | 73,664 tokens | — |
| AIME24 | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 10 launches × 10 built-in repeats per item; outer seed unset | on | 73,664 tokens | — |
| MMLU-Pro | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item | on | 65,536 tokens | — |
| GPQA Diamond | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 3 samples per item | on | 73,664 tokens | — |
| CRUXEval (output) | Evalchemy | accuracy (output) | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item | off | 73,664 tokens | — |
| FinanceBench | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item | off | 73,664 tokens | — |
| IFBench | Evalchemy | strict prompt-level accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per item | off | 73,664 tokens | — |
| MRCR | Evalchemy | mean sequence similarity | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per selected item | off | model-specific; at most 73,728 tokens | — |
| NUPA (full tracker protocol) | Evalchemy | accuracy | 0 | 1 run × 1 sample per 238,926 selected items | model default | 73,664 tokens | — |
| SWE-bench Verified random-100 | Harbor / Terminus-2 | accuracy | 0 | 1 agent trial per task | model default | 32,768 tokens | — |
| OpenThoughts-TBLite 2.0 | Harbor / Terminus-2 | accuracy | 0 | 1 agent trial per task | model default | 32,768 tokens | — |
| Terminal-Bench 2.0 | Harbor / Terminus-2 | accuracy | 0 | 1 agent trial per task | model default | 32,768 tokens | — |
| DS-1000 mini-200 | Harbor / Terminus-2 | accuracy | 0 | 1 agent trial per task | model default | 32,768 tokens | — |
| BFCL-Parity @ Pi | Harbor / Pi | accuracy | 0 | 1 agent trial per task | model default | 32,768 tokens | — |
| BixBench CLI corrections @ Pi | Harbor / Pi | accuracy | 0 | 1 agent trial per task | model default | 32,768 tokens | — |
| τ³-bench @ Pi | Harbor / Pi ACP | accuracy | 0 | 1 agent trial per task | model default | 32,768 tokens | — |
| SOTOPIA-hard | Harbor / SOTOPIA agent | normalized goal achievement | 0 | 1 episode per scenario | model default | 32,768 tokens | — |

### Out of Distribution

* AAII 4.3
* Harbor-Index
* Terminal-Bench Science
* DeepSWE 1.1 (deep-swe-litecontainer@1.1)

### Details on our Evals

- **MATH-500.** OpenAI's [May 2023 process-supervision release](https://openai.com/index/improving-mathematical-reasoning-with-process-supervision/) used a 500-problem subset of the original MATH competition-math benchmark. The campaign scores one zero-shot generated solution per problem by final-answer accuracy.
- **HumanEval+.** The [May 2023 EvalPlus paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210) introduced expanded tests for HumanEval programs to catch incorrect code that passes sparse original tests. The campaign executes one zero-shot completion per problem against the stronger tests.
- **MBPP+.** The [November 24, 2023 EvalPlus release](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus/releases/tag/v0.2.0) extends MBPP with additional functional tests. The campaign's pinned config is zero-shot and scores one generated program per problem.
- **OlympiadBench.** The [February 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14008) introduced bilingual, multimodal Olympiad-level math and science problems. This campaign uses Evalchemy's 30-question text subset, ten sampled solutions per question, and the configured answer judge.
- **GSM8K.** The [October 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168) introduced grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic. The campaign uses the zero-shot `gsm8k-0shot` completion route and scores the extracted final answer.
- **PIQA.** The [November 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11641) introduced two-choice questions about physical commonsense. The campaign selects the answer by length-normalized log-likelihood with no examples in the prompt.
- **WinoGrande.** The [July 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10641) introduced adversarial pronoun/coreference choices designed to reduce superficial cues. The campaign uses five-shot multiple-choice scoring.
- **BoolQ.** The [May 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10044) introduced naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with evidence passages. The campaign scores zero-shot choice accuracy.
- **TruthfulQA MC2.** The [September 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07958) introduced questions that elicit common misconceptions from language models. The campaign's MC2 metric sums probability mass on all true answers within each question's candidate set, rather than counting a single selected answer.
- **TriviaQA.** The [May 2017 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03551) introduced trivia questions with independently collected evidence documents. The campaign runs five-shot answer generation and reports answer accuracy.
- **AIME24.** The [Mathematical Association of America's 2024 AIME](https://maa.org/maa-invitational-competitions/) supplies the contest problems; AIME24 is a year-specific evaluation set, not a separately introduced research benchmark. Evalchemy samples ten solutions per question through the benchmark's built-in repeat loop and scores the integer final answers. The campaign ran that 30-question, ten-repeat protocol ten times, for 3,000 generations per model. The preserved launch records have `evalchemy.seed: null`, so the outer launches were not ten distinct random seeds; every launch used the same benchmark-internal repeat seed schedule.
- **MMLU-Pro.** The [June 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01574) introduced harder, more reasoning-focused multiple-choice questions across fourteen subjects. The campaign runs zero-shot generation with a 65,536-token cap and reports micro-averaged accuracy.
- **GPQA Diamond.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) introduced expert-written graduate-level science questions, including the Diamond subset. The campaign averages accuracy over three generated answers per question.
- **CRUXEval (output).** The [January 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03065) introduced input- and output-prediction tasks for short Python programs. The tracker reports the output-prediction direction, scored on one generated answer per item.
- **FinanceBench.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11944) introduced questions grounded in public financial filings. The campaign scores one generated answer per question with its pinned LLM judge.
- **IFBench.** The [July 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02833) introduced verifiable constraints that test generalization in precise instruction following. The campaign reports strict prompt-level accuracy, requiring every constraint to hold in the raw response.
- **MRCR.** [Gemini's September 2024 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) introduced multi-round coreference resolution; [OpenAI's public MRCR release (April 2025)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr) supplies the corrected multi-needle data used here. The campaign scores nonce-gated sequence similarity and selects only context-length bins that fit the served model.
- **NUPA.** The [November 2024 Number Cookbook paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03766) introduced tests of numerical understanding and processing across representations and tasks. Existing tracker scores use the full Evalchemy protocol of 238,926 selected prompts.
- **SWE-bench Verified random-100.** OpenAI's [August 13, 2024 release](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) introduced a human-validated subset of repository-issue repair tasks. The campaign evaluates a fixed random 100-task subset of this existing subset, with one Terminus-2 trial per issue and executable verification.
- **OpenThoughts-TBLite 2.0.** The [February 18, 2026 release](https://www.openthoughts.ai/blog/openthoughts-tblite) introduced a 100-task, faster-running terminal-agent panel calibrated against Terminal-Bench 2. The campaign runs its pinned `openthoughts-tblite@2.0` tasks with Terminus-2 and reports verifier success.
- **Terminal-Bench 2.0.** The [November 7, 2025 release](https://www.tbench.ai/news/announcement-2-0) introduced a harder, more thoroughly verified terminal-agent task set alongside Harbor. The campaign uses the pinned TB2 dataset through Harbor with one Terminus-2 trial per task.
- **DS-1000 mini-200.** The [November 2022 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11501) introduced data-science code-generation problems spanning seven Python libraries. The campaign evaluates a fixed seed-42 200-task Harbor subset with Terminus-2, building task images from the pinned Dockerfiles.
- **BFCL-Parity @ Pi.** Berkeley's [February 2024 BFCL release](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html) introduced executable function-calling evaluation. This campaign uses the Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent, so its score is the pinned adaptation's verified solve rate rather than an unqualified BFCL leaderboard score.
- **BixBench CLI corrections @ Pi.** The [February 2025 BixBench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00096) introduced multi-step computational-biology analysis tasks. This campaign uses Pi on 205 `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` tasks and reports binary answer-equivalence reward, which is distinct from canonical BixBench CLI v1.5.
- **τ³-bench @ Pi.** Sierra's [March 18, 2026 τ³-Bench launch](https://sierra.ai/blog/bench-advancing-agent-benchmarking-to-knowledge-and-voice) introduced knowledge and voice tracks alongside corrections to the existing airline and retail tasks. The campaign runs pinned `tau3-bench@1.0.1` in Harbor through the Pi ACP relay and scores task verification.
- **SOTOPIA-hard.** The [October 2023 SOTOPIA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11667) introduced interactive social-agent evaluation and identified a hard scenario subset. The campaign runs the 100 hard episodes against a fixed `openai/gpt-oss-120b` counterpart and judge, then normalizes goal achievement from 0–10 to 0–1.

### How do we handle in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals?

#### IN-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- dedup against our SFT data, look at model scores while we develop the model, inspect the correlation of our ID evals with our OOD evals

**We may** -- develop synthetic RL tasks modeled on specific tasks in ID evals

**We will not** -- train on teacher rollouts from eval questions, use our ID eval instructions directly as the basis of RL data

#### OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- de-dup against our SFT raw data, look at meta-data about these evals (e.g., how big they are, general knowledge domain, etc), eval baselines on these evals

**We may** -- evaluate our final models on out-of-distribution benchmarks

**We will not** -- look at the individual questions in the evals, look at any of our own model scores from these evals until our model is frozen, model any synthetic tasks on tasks in the evals (edited)

### Metric definitions

- **`accuracy`:** the fraction of scored items that pass the benchmark's configured correctness check. The common name covers executable-test success for code and agent tasks, answer correctness for generated and multiple-choice tasks, FinanceBench's `correct` judge label, and BixBench's binary answer-equivalence check. NUPA counts an item as correct only when its format-specific extraction produces a representation-sensitive exact match. PIQA chooses the option with the highest length-normalized log-likelihood before testing correctness. AIME24 first averages its ten built-in repeats per question and then averages across ten outer launches; the outer launches did not pass distinct seeds. GPQA-Diamond and OlympiadBench average their three and ten in-run repeats per question. MMLU-Pro is micro-averaged across its fourteen subjects.
- **`mc2`:** TruthfulQA's probability mass on all true answers, normalized over the question's answer set and averaged over questions. It is not a binary selection accuracy, and chance performance is above zero.
- **`accuracy (output)`:** CRUXEval output-prediction accuracy. Given a function and input, the model predicts the output; this is distinct from CRUXEval input prediction, which reconstructs an input from the function and desired output.
- **`strict prompt-level accuracy`:** the fraction of IFBench prompts for which the raw response satisfies every required constraint.
- **`mean sequence similarity`:** MRCR's mean `SequenceMatcher` ratio between the response's answer span and the reference answer. A response that fails MRCR's nonce check receives zero credit. The standard 73,728-token serving window evaluates the published bins through 65,536 tokens. After Marin's 64-token serving safety margin, the 32,768-token models use bins through 16,384 and the 65,536-token model uses bins through 32,768. Those tracker cells are footnoted because differing bin coverage is not a strictly like-for-like comparison.
- **`normalized goal achievement`:** SOTOPIA-hard's official goal-achievement score for the evaluated character, linearly normalized from `[0, 10]` to `[0, 1]` and averaged over the 100 official hard episodes. The counterpart and evaluator are fixed to `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Together for every model.

### Other Metric Notes

- **Scale:** every metric in the suite is reported on a 0-1 scale with 1 the best and 0 the worst; there are no error counts, ranks, or unbounded scores.
- **Allowed context length:** This is allowed prompt + completion context length. If a model's maximum context length is less than the allowed context length, we adopt the model's maximum context length. For single-turn benchmarks, we subdivide the space into max prompt length = longest prompt in the dataset plus a bit of cushion, max response length = the remaining context window. For standard multi-turn benchmarks, max generation length per turn is capped at 8192. Context-ablation labels are `context window / per-turn output limit`: both values are passed explicitly, with the first applied to vLLM `max_model_len` and Pi `model_info.max_input_tokens`, and the second applied to Pi `model_info.max_output_tokens`. For example, `65k-16k` means a 65,536-token serving and Pi context window with a 16,384-token per-turn output limit.
- **Pi runtime:** Agentic Pi configs must pin `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` explicitly. The corrected context control pins Pi `0.87.0`; the original harness result used unpinned Pi `0.86.1`, while the first context-ablation rerun drifted to unpinned Pi `0.87.0`. Results from different Pi versions are not treated as a controlled context-only comparison.

### LLM judges

Four evals involve an LLM judge; every other eval in the suite grades programmatically
(IFBench verifies each constraint with its checker functions, MRCR uses `SequenceMatcher`,
the math evals use Minerva/SymPy, the multiple-choice evals compare selections, and the
harness/agentic evals run test suites).

- **FinanceBench:** every scored response is judged. The judge sees the question, the
  reference answers, and the candidate, and returns one label: `correct`, `incorrect`, or
  `not_attempted` (equivalent answers in substance count as correct — algebraic equivalence,
  unit conversions, rounding). Only `correct` scores.
- **BixBench CLI correction set:** every submitted answer is judged for semantic equivalence
  to the task's ideal answer and receives a binary reward. A missing answer receives zero
  without invoking the judge.
- **OlympiadBench:** Minerva/SymPy grades first, and the judge answers equivalence only for
  answers Minerva cannot establish; the reported scores come from the offline regrade, which
  uses this judge the same way (see "OlympiadBench regrade" below).
- **SOTOPIA-hard:** the official episode evaluator judges goal achievement for the evaluated
  character after each completed social interaction and returns the 0–10 score that the metric
  normalizes to 0–1.

The standard judge for all four is `openai/gpt-oss-120b` served through Together
(`JUDGE_MODEL`/`JUDGE_BASE_URL` in the launch commands; the credential is the Together API
key). Open weights and one model everywhere keep judge behavior consistent across evals and
runs, and reproducible anywhere Together (or a self-serve vLLM deployment of the same
checkpoint) is available. τ³'s LiteLLM client uses `openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b`: the first
segment selects LiteLLM's OpenAI-compatible provider and the remainder is Together's model ID.
Judge hyperparameters, per path:

- **Answer-equivalence judge** (FinanceBench, OlympiadBench): a single user message with the
  three-way rubric, `temperature=0`, request timeout 300 s with 5 transport retries, and 16
  concurrent judgments per run. `max_tokens` starts at 128 and escalates 128 → 512 → 2048
  when a completion comes back empty — a hosted reasoning model can spend a small completion
  budget on hidden reasoning and return no content — so the ladder guarantees the final label
  lands within budget. The context window is gpt-oss-120b's 131,072 tokens as served
  (Together); no truncation of the graded material happens judge-side. The raw completion is
  retained in the results for audit, alongside the parsed label.
- **BixBench verifier:** the verifier calls Chat Completions with `max_tokens=1024` and a
  structured response schema containing one boolean score. Sampling follows the endpoint's
  service defaults.
- **SOTOPIA evaluator:** the pinned SOTOPIA v0.1.5 evaluator uses the fixed judge model after
  each episode; the model under evaluation never acts as its own judge.

When a judge call fails after retries, the sample is recorded as grader infrastructure
failure (counted against the run's error tolerance) rather than silently scored zero.

### Thinking mode

The main table records the policy for every benchmark. `on` and `off` set
`enable_thinking` through the model or benchmark config; a benchmark override wins over the model
default. `model default` means the benchmark adds no override, and `not applicable` means the task
does not use a generated chat response. A setting has no effect when a model's template does not
support that control; gpt-oss-20b's Harmony reasoning channel is always on. Evalchemy
[`4d03c07d`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/4d03c07d0d9c0014b23d4447b6b95c0a5e4191e6)
forwards the resolved setting into chat requests.

### Errors and Exceptions

#### Infrastructure Error Tolerance

Modern benchmarks are prone to encountering transient infrastructure errors. Our policy is to allow a degree of tolerance for infrastructure error; up to 10% of a benchmark's tasks can be invalidated by an infrastructure failure before we invalidate the entire score for a model on the benchmark. We do not attempt to control for the particular infrastructure errors that were encountered by various models on particular tasks. For this reason, we report confidence intervals as slightly wider than they would be if all models had reported on all tasks.

#### Infrastructure vs Model Error

We categorize errors during the evaluation process as either infrastructure errors or model errors.
Model errors are scoreable and do not count toward the infrastructure-error threshold. Unless this
policy explicitly identifies an error as a model error, it is an infrastructure error.

For Harbor evals, the following error types are currently treated as score-able model errors.

- `AgentTimeoutError`: the agent reached its configured execution timeout; Harbor preserves
  the work produced so far and runs the verifier.
- `ContextLengthExceededError`: the model or agent exhausted the available context; Harbor
  treats that as a classified end to the attempt and runs the verifier.
- `TurnCapExhaustedError`: the agent reached its configured turn cap without declaring
  completion; Harbor runs the verifier on the resulting state.
- `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`: the agent process exited non-zero after potentially producing
  scoreable work; Harbor still runs the verifier. Agent-specific subclasses must be reported
  under their concrete exception type and reviewed for validity rather than silently grouped.

For these Harbor score-able model errors, we terminate the trial and then run the verifier on the output of the agent, if any output is present. Unlike the Evalchemy timeout rule above, we do *not* automatically score Harbor model errors as 0's. This is because sometimes, agents will solve the task correctly and then get stuck in a loop of self-doubt or fail to submit properly in their harness, and we regard that outcome as closer to a success than a failure.

#### Timeout Policy

The following limits apply to every policy benchmark; there are no benchmark-specific exceptions.

| Evaluator phase | Limit | Outcome when the limit expires |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Evalchemy trial | 30 minutes | Record `0.0` as an `AgentTimeoutError`. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor agent setup | 6 minutes | Record `AgentSetupTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |
| Harbor agent execution | 30 minutes | Record `AgentTimeoutError`, preserve the agent's work, and run the verifier. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor verifier | 5 minutes | Record `VerifierTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |

The Evalchemy limit covers the full trial, including request retries and backoff, after the trial
acquires an evaluator slot. Evalchemy [#175](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/175)
implements the deadline, and campaign configs set `timeout=1800`.

Harbor launch configs override task-manifest values with
`agents[].override_setup_timeout_sec: 360`, `agents[].override_timeout_sec: 1800`, and
`verifier.override_timeout_sec: 300`. `artifacts/common.sh` checks these values before submission,
so the same limits apply even when a task manifest omits its own timeout.

## Baseline Models

### How we select baseline models

The process for selecting baseline models in our policy is fundamentally heuristic and community-driven. For each new model release, we will strive to select a representative cohort of open-weights and open-source models that are roughly comparable to Marin models and document them in the policy. We will look up reported results for those models in the research literature and, where available, use them as targets for internal reproduction, noting, however, that typically the variance in hyperparameters will make published results not directly comparable to our own. We will sometimes substitute quantized variants of the listed models for the canonical models, especially for larger models where our hardware makes it challenging to run inference on the non-quantized variants.

## Run resumption

Resume an interrupted Harbor run only when its model, evaluator pins, runtime limit, and dataset
state are unchanged. Find the Iris root in `artifacts/config-snapshots/launches.jsonl`, then use
that snapshot's `launch.json` and copied YAML files. Replay its saved arguments with only the
affected Harbor config, retaining any `--limit` and `--records-prefix`, and add the original run ID:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config artifacts/config-snapshots/launches/<snapshot-id>/<model-config>.yaml \
  --harbor-config artifacts/config-snapshots/launches/<snapshot-id>/<harbor-config>.yaml \
  --resume-run-id <original-run-id>
```

The durable `<records-prefix>/<original-run-id>/results/harbor_jobs/` tree must remain accessible.
Harbor preserves completed scored trials and reruns missing attempts and exceptions in its pinned
resume taxonomy. Use a clean replacement when model, policy, pins, limits, records prefix, or
dataset state changed, or when the unscored error is outside that taxonomy. Never delete a trial
directory to force recovery.

## Baseline-specific launch settings

The YAML files under `artifacts/model-configs/` are authoritative for checkpoint and tokenizer
revisions, serving context, GPU count, tensor and data parallelism, reasoning parser, tool parser,
sampling overrides, and Pi `thinking_format`. Use the matching file unchanged. Pi uses
`qwen-chat-template` for Qwen3.6 and Qwen3-Next and `chat-template` for the other models.

MRCR serves at 73,728 tokens and gives Evalchemy 73,664 after its 64-token safety margin. Ling
Lite's native 32,768-token window uses `mrcr-32k.yaml`; the historical 65,536-token Snowball
candidate uses `mrcr-65k.yaml`; every release-figure model uses `mrcr.yaml` otherwise. Evalchemy
evaluates only the published bins that fit.

K2 Horizon adds `--chat-template-content-format string` to vLLM. Its OlympiadBench, TriviaQA,
MMLU-Pro, and GPQA-Diamond runs use eight H100s, tensor parallelism 2, data parallelism 4, a 512 GiB
serve-worker memory request, and 16 concurrent Evalchemy requests. The serve settings are in
`artifacts/model-configs/IFM-K2-Horizon-MoVA-36B-A4B.yaml`; the evaluator command sets concurrency,
and the immutable launch snapshots preserve both.

## Updating codebase pins

Use the newest campaign pin for each codebase across the full release, assuming forward
compatibility with earlier score-producing runs. If a pin change causes an observed result
regression, stop launches, fix or revert the change, and issue a new policy version when the
evaluation behavior intentionally changes. Preserve the original run's exact pins in its immutable
config snapshot even after the release-wide pins advance.

## Standards for presenting Marin evals

* Select the release Snowball checkpoint by simple paired benchmark win rate among Snowball candidates. Release figures include only the selected checkpoint, not the other Snowball candidates. The Snowball candidate family includes the Grug 67B A2B checkpoint as well as checkpoints named Snowball. For each benchmark, plot the selected Snowball checkpoint and every non-Snowball baseline with an available score and total-training-FLOP estimate. Performance is on the y-axis and total training FLOPs are on a logarithmic x-axis. A baseline with an incomplete suite may appear in the scatterplots for its completed benchmarks, but it is excluded from cross-benchmark critical-difference analysis unless it has the full common benchmark panel.
* Produce uncertainty-aware normalized critical-difference diagrams with and without a FLOP control. Normalize scores within each benchmark across the complete-panel cohort. Estimate each score's task-level sample SEM from the scored trial rewards, then multiply the SEM by `1 / sqrt(0.9)` to account conservatively for the policy's 10% infrastructure-failure tolerance. With a fixed random seed, draw 100,000 score panels from independent normal sampling distributions centered on the reported scores and clipped to the metric's `[0, 1]` range. Rank models within every benchmark for each draw, using average ranks for ties, and report mean ranks with simultaneous 95% bands based on the draw-wise maximum absolute rank deviation. Report the Nemenyi critical difference at `alpha = 0.05`; it depends on the number of models and benchmarks, while score uncertainty affects the simulated rank distribution and its simultaneous bands.
* For the FLOP-controlled diagram, regress the draw's benchmark-normalized scores on `log10(total training FLOPs)` with one common linear slope, rank the within-benchmark residuals, and otherwise use the same uncertainty procedure. Treat FLOP estimates as fixed point estimates and disclose that their estimation uncertainty is not propagated. The uncontrolled diagram ranks the sampled normalized scores directly.
* We use a 6ND proxy for pretraining FLOPS, and 6 * max_tokens_per_rollout / max_context_length * n_rollouts * active_params proxy for RL FLOPS; that said, we are the only lab, as of this writing, which releases RL FLOPS, so meaningful comparisons are impossible. From the few labs who release midtraining / SFT information, we derive an unweighted mean percentage of FLOPS devoted to midtraining. We then estimate midtraining FLOPS for other labs using that mean. We estimate total FLOPS as the sum of pretraining FLOPS + (all midtraining / non-RL) FLOPS + (all RL and OPD) FLOPS. For any model which doesn't give sufficient evidence for any of the three stages, use the mean FLOPS over all models in the cohort as the estimated  FLOPS for that stage.
* In a separate standalone table, include all raw scores in XX.y format, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the trial count and the infrastructure error tolerance -- do not leave gaps, use table captions for results that require further context, use the exact same model family in the table as was present in the x-y scatterplot(s)
* Eval results are reportable IFF the eval in question completed with <10% of trials encountering infrastructure errors
* Eval results are reportable IFF they include provenance, in the form of model traces, and where available, verifier traces
* Any eval result that is publicly presented should clearly distinguish whether the benchmarks are in-distribution (part of the dev set), held out, or a mix of the two
* Any eval result that is publicly presented in a major release should report on *all* ID and OOD benchmarks, avoiding cherry picking, substitution, or new evals outside of a formal policy update
* For active development and internal communication, it is fine to define working subsets of the ID benchmarks and report on those in isolation

## Future considerations

* We would like to post-train multiple Snowball checkpoints, experimenting with different degrees of compute applied to post-training, to establish trade-off lines / domains
* We would like to think about a "marin model card" that would set minimum standards for true open development
* amd/Instella-MoE-16B-A3B-Think is not runnable currently from our pinned vLLM fork, but we would like to look at this model in the future

spillover_issues.body:
🤖

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment investigated why Delphi p33m67 K=0.20 math midtraining looked badly mispredicted at 1e22 FLOPs on the old `nemotron_cc_math_v1/4plus` validation target. The evidence points to a validation and measurement confound rather than a real scaling-law break: the old split contained fuzzy near-duplicate math documents, and K=0.20 gives larger base models many more midtraining tokens, so contamination exposure grows with scale and math fraction. Fixed-token iso-token controls stayed smooth, and the actual-seen clean validation set reduced the p33m67 K=0.20 1e22 endpoint error from about +18.6% on the old target to +2.83%, while the dropped contaminated complement retained the large miss. The current recommendation is to treat old 4plus as a historical contaminated baseline and use actual-seen clean validation plus fixed-token iso-token ladders for endpoint-fit sanity checks; per-mix clean validation remains the stricter follow-up if p50m50/p67m33 conclusions need to be finalized.

### Helpful links
- Original Delphi midtraining report: https://ahmeda14960.github.io/delphi-midtraining/?v=c86be93c
- Contamination logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/deconamint/.agents/logbooks/nemotron_math_data.md
- Final seen-partition plots and artifact branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6742#issuecomment-3016159353
- Stable figure bundle: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/issue-6742-midtraining-plots/docs/reports/figures/midtraining_validation_contamination
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

This issue tracks the Delphi math-midtraining validation-contamination investigation and the follow-up clean-seen evaluations. It follows from #4547, where the K=0.20 p33m67 ladder originally looked too good at 1e22 on the old `nemotron_cc_math_v1/4plus` validation target.

## Hypothesis or Goal

We want to determine whether the large 1e22 prediction miss came from a real midtraining scaling break or from confounds in the evaluation target and token budget. The working conclusion is that the old target was confounded by scale-dependent exposure to near-duplicate math documents, and the error mostly disappears on fixed-token or actual-seen-clean validation targets.

### Links

* Prior tracking issue: #4547
* Original public report: https://ahmeda14960.github.io/delphi-midtraining/?v=c86be93c
* Contamination branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/deconamint
* Contamination logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/deconamint/.agents/logbooks/nemotron_math_data.md
* Local final retrospective: `.agents/logbooks/midtraining_prediction_final.md`

## Results

The old K=0.20 p33m67 1e22 math-validation miss was about +18.6% on the old 4plus target. Fixed-token iso-token ladders had small 1e22 errors, around -3% to -4%, on the old target. The actual-seen clean validation target reduced the K=0.20 p33m67 1e22 error to +2.83% for lr0.50, and the retained-clean seen-partition plot shows low-single-digit error while the dropped contaminated complement retains a large absolute miss.

## TL;DR

The evidence supports a validation/measurement confound rather than a broken midtraining scaling law. K=0.20 is not a pure FLOP axis; it gives larger base models many more midtraining tokens. The old math validation split also had fuzzy near-duplicate and same-source leakage. Both effects grow with scale and math fraction.

## Scope

This issue covers Delphi p33m67/p50m50/p67m33 math midtraining, K=0.20 iso-FLOP runs, iso-token controls, Nemotron math validation contamination scans, decontaminated validation sets, clean-seen evals, and seen-partition complement evals.

## Decision log

* 2026-06-03: exact duplicate contamination was ruled out; fuzzy near-duplicate contamination was found.
* 2026-06-07: decontaminated eval sweeps showed scale-dependent contamination effects.
* 2026-06-15: 4plus-only decon sets and perplexity-gap mechanism plots confirmed high-J documents become unusually easy at 1e22.
* 2026-06-21: iso-token endpoint scaling showed fixed-token ladders are smooth.
* 2026-06-28: clean-seen and seen-partition analyses made the contamination explanation the best current account.

## Negative results index

* More flexible Chinchilla/log-log/resource-axis fits did not fix the old K=0.20 target.
* Separate base-loss components did not explain the old target anomaly.
* Base-model step-0 math loss was smooth; the anomaly appears after midtraining exposure.

## Current baseline

Use the actual-seen clean validation set and the fixed-token iso-token ladders for endpoint-fit sanity checks. Treat the old 4plus validation anchor as a contaminated historical baseline, not as the primary target for deciding whether midtraining scaling is smooth.

comments.body:
🤖 Update: contamination scan and exposure replay

Change:
- Reconstructed the old math validation split from the tokenized `nemotron_cc_math_v1/4plus` cache.
- Scanned the training side for fuzzy near-duplicates of validation documents.
- Replayed actual K=0.20 math exposure by scale and mix.

Result:
- Exact duplicate doc hashes across the 45.1M-doc corpus: 0.
- Fuzzy near-duplicates were common. At verified 5-char-shingle Jaccard >= 0.75:
  - 9,757 / 57,243 validation docs had at least one train near-duplicate.
  - 6,839 / 12,500 validation windows touched those docs.
  - 9.53M / 51.20M validation tokens were implicated.

The K=0.20 exposure replay showed the contamination opportunity grows with scale for p33m67:

| Scale | Combined exposed validation tokens |
|---|---:|
| 3e18 | 0.635M |
| 3e20 | 5.755M |
| 1e21 | 10.282M |
| 1e22 | 20.165M |

At 1e22 the exposure also tracked the math fraction:

| Mix | Combined exposed validation tokens |
|---|---:|
| p33m67 | 20.165M |
| p50m50 | 17.281M |
| p67m33 | 14.015M |

Interpretation:
- The deterministic Feistel split made validation identity reproducible, but it did not fuzzy-deduplicate source documents before the train/val split.
- K=0.20 is an iso-FLOP fraction, not a fixed-token condition. Larger base models receive many more midtraining tokens, so they have more chances to see near-twins of old validation docs.
- The old target anomaly was strongest exactly where this mechanism predicts: larger scale and higher math fraction.

Mechanism evidence:
- Decon cutoff sweeps showed the old anchor vs decon gap changes with scale.
- Per-document/per-token scoring showed high-J documents become unusually easy at 1e22. In one curated j088 example, median token loss collapsed from about 1.99 to 0.003 nats, and 78% of tokens were below 0.05 nats at 1e22.

comments.author: ahmeda14960
comments.body:
🤖 **Update — Nemotron-CC-Math benchmark decontamination against MATH500, GSM8K, and AIME24**

Moving this update here because this is the validation/contamination tracking issue; the earlier midtraining-recipe issue is not the right place for this detail.

I added and ran a reproducible benchmark decontamination pipeline for `nemotron_cc_math_v1/4plus` against the math benchmark sources we care about here. Code is pushed on branch `deconamint` at `6718716443`.

**Corpus scanned**

Every split was run against the same normalized Nemotron-CC-Math 4plus corpus:

```text
gs://marin-us-east5/normalized/nemotron_cc_math_v1/4plus_b05688a8/outputs/main
```

That corpus has `45,096,087` normalized documents. All jobs ran in `us-east5` to avoid cross-region reads.

**Eval sources we decontaminated against**

The benchmark data was first staged into a Datakit-readable directory, one JSONL gzip per split, with `id` and rendered `text` fields plus a hidden manifest sidecar:

```text
gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir
```

Exact staged inputs:

| split key | dataset | revision | config | split | staged file | records |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| `math500__test` | `HuggingFaceH4/MATH-500` | `ff5b202` | n/a | `test` | `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/math500/test/data.jsonl.gz` | 500 |
| `gsm8k__main__train` | `openai/gsm8k` | `740312add88f781978c0658806c59bc2815b9866` | `main` | `train` | `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/gsm8k/main/train/data.jsonl.gz` | 7,473 |
| `gsm8k__main__test` | `openai/gsm8k` | `740312add88f781978c0658806c59bc2815b9866` | `main` | `test` | `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/gsm8k/main/test/data.jsonl.gz` | 1,319 |
| `aime24__train` | `HuggingFaceH4/aime_2024` | `2fe88a2f1091d5048c0f36abc874fb997b3dd99a` | n/a | `train` | `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/aime24/train/data.jsonl.gz` | 30 |

Rendering details: MATH500/AIME24 rows are rendered as problem + solution + answer; GSM8K rows are rendered as question + answer. The staging script is `scripts/analysis/stage_math_decontam_sources.py`.

**How the Datakit decontamination pass works**

The main driver is `scripts/analysis/decon_nemotron_math_against_benchmarks.py`. It runs one independent Datakit pass per eval split. This is intentional: a combined Bloom filter would answer “contaminated by any benchmark,” but would not give a clean per-benchmark contamination report.

Settings used for each split:

```text
ngram_length = 13
ngram_stride = 0
overlap_threshold = 0.5
false_positive_rate = 1e-9
max_workers = 256
worker_cpu = 2
worker_ram = 6g
```

Important semantic detail: this Datakit path is **not MinHash/LSH Jaccard**. It is exact word-ngram containment through a Bloom filter:

1. Datakit splits each eval record text into newline paragraphs.
2. It inserts every contiguous 13-word eval n-gram hash into a Bloom filter and writes `_bloom/eval_hash_index.parquet` so matched hashes can be attributed back to eval IDs.
3. For each Nemotron source document, it scores each source paragraph as:

   ```text
   datakit_score(paragraph)
     = (# source paragraph 13-word n-gram positions that hit the eval Bloom)
       / (# source paragraph 13-word n-gram positions)
   ```

4. It writes one row per Nemotron document. A document is marked contaminated when the maximum paragraph score in that document is at least `0.5`.

So the output is **document-labeled but paragraph-scored**: the whole Nemotron document is flagged if any paragraph has >=50% of its contiguous 13-word n-gram positions present in the eval split.

**Contamination results**

Aggregate reports:

```text
gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/decon_nemotron_cc_math_4plus/contamination_report.all.json
gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/decon_nemotron_cc_math_4plus/contamination_report.all.csv
```

| split | eval records | eval records hit | contaminated Nemotron docs | contamination rate over 45,096,087 docs | mean contaminated max overlap | max overlap |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `math500__test` | 500 | 141 | 11,868 | 0.00026317139223188036 | 0.6397847284198739 | 1.0 |
| `gsm8k__main__train` | 7,473 | 146 | 1,224 | 0.000027142044497120115 | 0.7504422749907789 | 1.0 |
| `gsm8k__main__test` | 1,319 | 32 | 123 | 0.00000272750937348511 | 0.8405145245892016 | 1.0 |
| `aime24__train` | 30 | 17 | 18 | 0.00000039914771319294287 | 0.9457209585052948 | 1.0 |

Per-split Datakit attributes and reports live under:

```text
gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/decon_nemotron_cc_math_4plus/<split>/datakit_decon_attrs
gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/decon_nemotron_cc_math_4plus/<split>/contamination_report.json
```

**How we recover the offending documents**

After Datakit marks documents, `scripts/analysis/export_decon_contaminated_docs.py` reads only the Datakit attribute parquets and `_bloom/eval_hash_index.parquet`. It does not rescan the source text. It exports a compact manifest of only contaminated documents, including:

- normalized document `id`
- `source_parquet`
- `partition_id`
- `row_index_in_partition`
- Datakit `max_overlap`
- matched Bloom hashes
- matched benchmark eval IDs

Output pattern:

```text
gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/decon_nemotron_cc_math_4plus/<split>/contaminated_docs/contaminated_docs.parquet
```

Those fields are enough to recover the exact normalized source document later: `source_parquet` + `row_index_in_partition` points to the row in the Nemotron normalized parquet.

**Extra exact Jaccard/localization pass after finding offenders**

The Datakit pass is optimized for broad marking, not human inspection. After we know the offending document IDs/rows, we run a targeted exact localization pass with `scripts/analysis/localize_decon_contaminated_docs.py`.

This second pass reads only the contaminated source rows and the corresponding staged eval split. It re-extracts the same 13-word n-grams exactly, without the Bloom filter, and computes direct overlap metrics:

```text
source containment
  = source paragraph hit positions / source paragraph n-gram positions

source-unique containment
  = |source paragraph unique n-grams ∩ eval unique n-grams| / |source paragraph unique n-grams|

record Jaccard
  = |source paragraph unique n-grams ∩ eval record unique n-grams|
    / |source paragraph unique n-grams ∪ eval record unique n-grams|
```

It also searches eval paragraphs to find the best matching eval paragraph for each source paragraph, stores source/eval character spans, snippets, and sampled shared 13-word n-grams. This is the extra “Jaccard check” layer: Datakit decides the contaminated-doc set by paragraph containment; the localization pass then verifies and explains the overlaps with exact set-based metrics and coordinates.

This distinction matters because the Datakit threshold is containment, not Jaccard. A source paragraph can have >=50% of its n-grams contained in a much larger eval record while the Jaccard against the full eval record is lower. That is why the localization table reports exact Jaccard separately instead of treating Datakit `max_overlap` as Jaccard.

Localized overlap outputs:

```text
gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/decon_nemotron_cc_math_4plus/<split>/localized_overlaps/localized_overlaps.parquet
gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/decon_nemotron_cc_math_4plus/<split>/localized_overlaps/summary.json
```

Localization summary:

| split | contaminated docs | localized docs | localized rows | localization misses | max exact record Jaccard |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `math500__test` | 11,868 | 11,868 | 13,797 | 0 | 0.8974358974358975 |
| `gsm8k__main__train` | 1,224 | 1,224 | 1,437 | 0 | 1.0 |
| `gsm8k__main__test` | 123 | 123 | 309 | 0 | 1.0 |
| `aime24__train` | 18 | 18 | 103 | 0 | 0.4188034188034188 |

All four splits had zero localization misses: every Datakit-flagged contaminated document had an exact localized overlap at the targeted threshold when checked against the attributed eval records.

**Inspection viewer**

I also built a combined static HTML viewer with a dataset dropdown so we can inspect source/eval snippets and highlighted shared n-grams:

```text
gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/ahmed/math-decontamin-dir/decon_nemotron_cc_math_4plus/localized_overlap_viewer.html
```

Local generation command:

```bash
uv run python scripts/analysis/build_localized_overlap_viewer.py
```

The viewer is just a static inspection layer over the `localized_overlaps.parquet` files. It does not reread the 45M-doc corpus; the durable source coordinates are in the localized parquet rows.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

In Iris multi-backend mode, each task backend owns its live worker inventory and
placement (which attempt runs on which worker). The in-process RPC backend keeps
this in a local store, and the design rule is: a backend's worker/placement store
is a **cache**, not durable truth. If a backend loses it, that is treated as "all
tasks were lost" — the controller's durable record (`task X is assigned/running on
backend Y`) re-routes the work through the normal reschedule path — never as a
fatal reconcile error.

The one thing blocking a fully store-free RPC backend is the worker reconcile
protocol. Today `ReconcileRequest.desired` is documented as the *complete expected
set*, and a worker stops any local attempt whose UID is absent from it
(`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py`, `lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/worker.proto`).
A backend that comes up with an empty placement store would therefore tell every
worker to stop everything before it could re-learn what is running.

Add an observe-before-converge (recovery) path to the worker reconcile protocol so
a freshly-started backend can learn the attempts a worker is running *without*
issuing stops, then re-adopt them. With that, the RPC backend's placement store
becomes a pure cache rebuildable from live worker reports + provider state, and the
backend can run with no durable local DB at all.

This overlaps the multi-backend recovery work (the level-triggered reconcile +
epoch fence, "PR4" of the program); file it so the store-free-backend endpoint is
tracked on its own.

### Definition of Done

- The worker reconcile protocol supports an observe-only / recovery phase: a backend
  learns running attempts from worker reports without those reports being read as a
  desired-set teardown.
- A backend that starts with an empty placement store re-adopts the attempts its
  workers report rather than stopping them.
- The in-process RPC backend can run with an ephemeral (non-durable) placement store.
- Covered by a restart test: wipe the backend's placement store mid-run; running
  attempts survive and are re-adopted.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 This is design-stage, multi-module work (proto change + worker reconcile + backend recovery + ephemeral store + restart test) that **overlaps the in-flight multi-backend "PR4" program** (design #6718; impl #6730, #6731). The RPC backend's placement store referenced in the DoD does not exist on `main` yet — it lands with those PRs. Per the agent scope rule (>100 LOC / multi-module / design), no PR; posting root cause + a proposed approach for a human to review and sequence against PR4.

# Research

The only thing forcing a backend to keep durable placement is the reconcile protocol's *complete-desired-set* semantics. `ReconcileRequest` carries `worker_id` + `desired` and nothing else; the worker treats any non-terminal local attempt whose UID is **absent** from `desired` as a zombie and kills it. A backend that restarts with an empty placement store sends an empty `desired` and tells every worker to stop everything before it can re-learn what is running.

**Relevant code**
- [`worker.proto#L73-L76`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/worker.proto#L73-L76) — `ReconcileRequest`, `desired` = "complete expected set"
- [`worker.py#L871-L881`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L871-L881) — zombie-kill: absent-from-`desired` ⇒ `_kill_async`
- [`worker.py#L889-L911`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L889-L911) — observations bounded to `desired` ∪ zombies (won't surface unknown-to-backend attempts)
- [`reconcile/worker.py#L110-L221`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reconcile/worker.py#L110-L221) — `build_reconcile_plans` builds `desired` from durable state
- [`controller/backend.py#L340-L363`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/backend.py#L340) — `TaskBackend` protocol (where the RPC backend + its placement store hangs)

The existing worker-side container adoption ([`worker.py#L319-L398`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L319-L398)) recovers attempts across a *worker* restart; this issue is the symmetric case for a *backend* restart, and needs a protocol affordance rather than local container scanning.

# Proposed Approach

**1. Add an observe-only phase to the reconcile protocol.** Add a field to `ReconcileRequest` — `bool observe_only = 3;` (or a `ReconcileMode mode` enum if more phases are foreseen). When set, the worker:
  - skips the zombie-kill loop ([`worker.py#L871-L881`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L871-L881)) — absence is *not* a stop signal;
  - still applies explicit `run`/`stop` intents (so a recovering backend can keep handing out specs);
  - reports its **complete** non-terminal attempt set in `observed`, not just the desired∩local subset ([`worker.py#L889-L911`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/worker.py#L889-L911)).

This makes the absent-UID case mean "I don't know yet," distinct from today's "stop this."

**2. Backend recovery (observe → adopt → converge).** A backend that comes up with an empty placement store runs an observe-only sweep across its workers, rebuilds placement from `observed` attempt UIDs cross-referenced with the controller's durable `task assigned/running on backend Y` record (and provider state), then flips to normal converge mode. Attempts the durable record disowns fall out through the existing reschedule path — never a fatal reconcile error.

**3. Ephemeral placement store.** Once placement is rebuildable from live worker reports + provider state, the in-process RPC backend's store becomes a pure cache and can be non-durable. This piece lands against the RPC backend introduced in #6730/#6731.

**4. Test.** Restart test: with attempts running, wipe the backend's placement store mid-run; assert running attempts are observed and re-adopted (not stopped) and that no `stop`/zombie-kill is issued during the observe phase. A focused worker-level test (`tests/cluster/worker/test_reconcile.py`) can assert that an `observe_only` reconcile with empty `desired` returns the full observed set and kills nothing.

**Sequencing question for a human:** steps 1–2 (protocol + worker semantics) are independent of the RPC-backend store and could land first as a small, self-contained proto+worker change with the worker-level test. Steps 3–4 should ride on PR4 (#6730/#6731) where the store exists. Recommend splitting along that line unless PR4 owners want it bundled.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Goal

Test the boundary operator from [arXiv 2609.19107](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19107) ("How Model Growth, Recursion, and Boundary Operators Influence Scaling Exponents") on the grug MoE block, at matched parameters and FLOPs, before building any of the paper's looping/growth machinery.

The operator (paper's Operator-1, K=1, no looping, no growth): split the layers into prelude/core/coda (as even as possible; remainders to core first, then coda). The core starts from `h₀ = 0`, so its entry state is `BO(0, e) = α·e` where `e` is the prelude's output; after the last core block, the coda's entry state is `BO(h, e) = rms_norm(h) + α·e`. One RMSNorm and two vector-adds; zero new parameters.

Why this first: the paper reports the operator alone (no recursion, no growth) already moves the scaling exponent — effective compute multiplier ≈1.25× at 1e20 FLOPs. It is the cheapest decisive test of whether the paper's axes transfer to the MoE template: if the operator doesn't move the grug isoflop curves, looping/growth almost certainly won't either.

## Plan

- Variant `experiments/grug/moe_boundary/` copied from `experiments/grug/moe/` (copy-first per the grug archive workflow). Boundary-off is byte-identical to the parent (regression-tested on logits).
- Phase 0 arms at the four May Recipe compute-optimal cells (d512/3.82e17, d768/2.81e18, d1024/1.16e19, d1280/3.46e19), v4-32 EP=1, with the README measurement conditions pinned (seq 4096, PKO on, long RoPE on, z-loss off, batch/steps from the README table).
- d512 runs both α ∈ {1.0, 0.707} ("alpha insurance"; paper's tuned values for Operator-1 and Loop-2). Winner by final macro loss proceeds.
- Gate 1: effective speedup > 1 at d512 and d768 vs the README baselines (3.5422 @ 433,986 tok/s; 3.2273 @ 294,726).
- Gate 2: d1024 + d1280, refit `loss(C) = 1.6 + A·C^−α̂`, projections must beat 2.534 @ 1e21 and 2.205 @ 1e23; fitted α̂ vs 0.0941 is secondary evidence.
- Cost: ≈45 v4-32 slice-hours for the full phase; ≈7–8 for gate 1 alone.

## Records

Runs land in W&B project `marin_moe`, group `moe-boundary`. Results and the go/no-go call get recorded here as each gate resolves.

Part of #4281.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — scope: research experiment, no PR yet**

This is a multi-cell training experiment (variant + four v4-32 isoflop cells, two go/no-go gates, W&B recording), not a self-contained code fix. The workflow reserves PRs for small self-contained changes; larger/experiment work gets a reviewed approach first. Below is the grounded implementation design for the *code scaffolding* (the variant); launching the runs and resolving the gates is operator work (`use-iris` / grug launchers), not part of a code PR.

**Where the operator slots in.** The MoE forward loop iterates blocks linearly at [`model.py` L685–707](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7b63e0d0cefcb19282fd9cc7efb3c109cbfc4801/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L685-L707). Operator-1 (K=1, no loop/growth) wraps that loop:
- Split `self.blocks` into prelude / core / coda — even split, remainders to core first then coda.
- Run prelude on `hidden`; save `e = hidden` (prelude output).
- Core entry state `BO(0, e) = α·e` (core starts from `h₀=0`), so feed `α·e` into the first core block.
- After the last core block, coda entry state `BO(h, e) = rms_norm(h) + α·e`.
- Coda runs normally, then `final_norm` / `final_gated_norm` as today.

**Zero new parameters.** The paper's single RMSNorm is the existing non-parametric [`rms_norm` free function (`model.py` L252)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7b63e0d0cefcb19282fd9cc7efb3c109cbfc4801/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L252) — reuse it; do not add an `RMSNorm` module. The two adds are plain vector adds.

**Config knobs.** Add to `GrugModelConfig` ([`model.py` L95–133](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7b63e0d0cefcb19282fd9cc7efb3c109cbfc4801/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L95-L133)) a single `boundary_alpha: float | None = None`. `None` ⇒ boundary off ⇒ the forward path must be byte-identical to the parent (the "boundary-off" regression baseline the issue asks for). Set `0.707` (1/√2) or `1.0` to enable. Avoid a separate boolean + float pair (compound-state anti-pattern per AGENTS.md).

**Variant location.** Copy `experiments/grug/moe/` → `experiments/grug/moe_boundary/` (copy-first, per `change-grug` / grug archive workflow; the issue's own plan agrees). Keep edits local; no shared framework surface. Add a `docs/reports/grug-archive.md` entry (origin `moe`, purpose, status `active`, diff link from the CI diff comment).

**Test that earns its place.** One regression test: with `boundary_alpha=None`, logits are bitwise-equal to the parent `moe` model on a fixed seed/input (the issue's "byte-identical" claim). Optionally a shape/finiteness check with `boundary_alpha=0.707`. No tautological tests.

**Open questions before coding:**
1. Per-cell `num_layers` for d512/d768/d1024/d1280 come from the May Recipe README table — confirm the exact counts so the even prelude/core/coda split is well-defined (e.g. how a 6-layer cell splits: 2/2/2).
2. Confirm the split is by *block index* only (the attention long/short pattern at L688–690 stays keyed to absolute layer index `i`, unchanged by the operator).
3. Should `boundary_alpha` also thread through the HF config round-trip (`to_hf_config`/`from_hf_config`), or stay experiment-only? Recommend experiment-only until it proves out.

I can implement the variant + regression test as a scoped PR on request (code only; runs excluded). Want me to proceed with that, or adjust the design first?

Part of #4281.

comments.body:
🤖 **Phase 0 result: gate 1 FAILS at d512; debug ladder exhausted**

**Full d512 sweep** (Paloma macro loss / avg last-100-step tok/s):

| arm | macro loss | tok/s | compute mult |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline (README) | **3.5422** | 433,986 | 1.0 |
| α=1.0, LR ×1.0 | 3.5460 | 385,429 | 0.979 |
| α=0.707, LR ×1.0 | 3.5516 | 350,256 | 0.950 |
| α=1.0, LR ×0.5 | 3.5776 | 425,052 | 0.949 |
| α=1.0, LR ×2.0 | 3.6115 | 431,461 | 0.912 |

**Debug ladder (per the replication plan):**
- **α insurance**: α=1.0 wins (−5.6e-3 vs 0.707). Paper Table 5 agrees (Operator-1 αemb=1).
- **LR re-centering**: ×1.0 is the best of {0.5, 1, 2} — the May Recipe heuristic LR is already centered for this model; the paper's transfer regret is not recoverable by GLR alone. (Paper's regret comes from the full Stage-1 chain: ELRM/HLRM/RM/OM/WD/WTE/UIS/schedule/Adam — most of these knobs don't exist in the MoE template's MuonH.)
- **Split ratio**: 2/2/2 at d6 is the paper's validated optimum (even P/C/D, remainders core-then-coda; Table 4/Fig 15a show alternatives are worse).

**Verdict**: under the May Recipe MoE with the recipe transferred from the Vanilla-equivalent baseline, the boundary operator alone does **not** beat the baseline at d512 (deficit +3.8e-3 loss; throughput parity within noise — arms span 350k–431k tok/s at identical compute). This is consistent with the paper's transfer-regret finding (Table 6: Operator-1 under Vanilla's recipe loses 7.8e-3 at base size and erases the exponent improvement, Fig. 16b). It does *not* refute the paper — we measured the transferred-recipe condition by design (recipe-matched comparability with the README baselines).

**Consequences:**
- Gate 1 cannot pass (requires speedup > 1 at both d512 and d768), so d768/d1024/d1280 arms were **not** launched — saves ~35 v4-32 slice-hours of a failing protocol.
- Phase A (looping/growth) is not justified on top of a failed Phase 0: the paper's bigger gains (Untied-Grow 1.6–2.7×) compound the same recipe-transfer risk, and each ladder point is ~10× the cost of Phase 0.

**Options going forward** (needs a decision):
1. **Close as negative result** — BO alone is not a promotable recipe change for this template under recipe-matched conditions. Cheapest; PR #9281 still lands the (well-tested, off≡baseline-verified) variant for future use.
2. **Recipe refit for the BO** (paper-style Stage-1 tuning at d512: β₁/β₂/ε/warmup/WD sweeps, ~8–10 arms ≈ 13–16 slice-hours) — tests whether the regret is recoverable in this template at all before deciding on Phase A.
3. **Skip to a combined arm** (e.g. Untied-2) at one matched cell — the paper's headline gains are there, but a single arm can't separate BO-from-looping contributions without Phase 0 passing.

Artifacts: runs under W&B `marin_moe/moe-boundary`; analysis in `.agents/projects/boundary_loop.md`.
