comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 25: two-query AttnRes, blended AttnRes, and spreading the MoE input** (branch `ladderclimb_v1_batch14`, d512, paired against the current best, 3.0834)

These follow up [the two-query / λ-blend comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5844691943) and [the MLP input-spread comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5844712356). Every flag defaults off. The changes apply to every AttnRes gate, including the final one.

**Two queries per gate (`attn_res_dual_query`).** Each gate keeps its zero-init query `q_a` and adds a second query `q_b ~ N(0, σ)`, so both start close to an even mix over the sources.
- Each query takes its own softmax-weighted sample of the sources, giving `mix_a` and `mix_b`.
- Merge per token: `s = σ(rms_norm(stream) · w + b)`, input = `s · mix_a + (1 − s) · mix_b`. Here `stream` is the plain sum of the gate's sources.
- `w` and `b` are zero-init, so `s = ½` at init.
- σ is tried at 0.005 and 0.02. The initial logit spread is about σ·√D, i.e. 0.11 and 0.45.

**Blend with the standard residual (`attn_res_blend`).** Input = `λ₁ · attnres_mix + λ₂ · mean(sources)`, with learned scalars per gate, both init 1.
- I used the mean rather than the sum. The RMSNorm that follows makes the two equivalent, apart from how λ₂ is parameterized.
- **static:** λ are plain scalars.
- **dynamic:** λₖ also gets `+ rms_norm(stream) · wₖ`, a zero-init per-token term.
- Caveat: at init the AttnRes mix *is* the uniform mean, and the following RMSNorm cancels scale. So the λ gradient is about 0 until the gate moves off uniform. The params are on Adam, which rescales small gradients, so they will still move.

**MLP input spread.** Here is how I read the idea. How well a neuron can choose which fraction of tokens it fires on depends on the spread of `w·x`. If `x` sits on a small, anisotropic manifold (a large shared mean direction and a few dominant directions), most `w` see little variance, and the high-variance directions dominate learning.
- **Whitening** the input (`x → C^{-1/2}(x − μ)`) makes every direction carry unit variance, so any `w` sees the same spread.
- For a linear layer that follows, whitening is a reparameterization of `W`, so it adds no expressivity. It changes what Adam and Muon do: it is K-FAC's / Shampoo's input-side factor applied to the activations. Muon orthogonalizes the update but ignores the input covariance, so that factor is what our optimizer is missing.
- It also changes the router, since QB reads the whitened input.
- The matching knobs:
  - **center:** subtract the batch mean (over all tokens, stop-gradient) from every MoE input.
  - **whiten, p:** `x → (x − μ) · C^{−p/2}`, with `C` the batch covariance. Its eigenvalues are trace-normalized, then shrunk by `+1e-3`, via `eigh` on a 512×512 matrix. Stop-gradient, so there is no backward through `eigh`. p = 0.5 is half-whitening (Shampoo's exponent); p = 1 is full ZCA whitening.
- Caveats:
  - Batch statistics leak about 1/N of each token into all others (N ≈ 130k tokens), and eval uses the eval batch's own statistics. If whitening wins, I'll switch to EMA statistics from previous steps, which are strictly causal.
  - These runs are **data-matched** (2817 steps). If one wins, I'll check its throughput and fixed-time step count.

Other ideas for the spread question (not yet run): a spread penalty on the MoE input's covariance (for example log-det or effective rank), an EMA-whitened version as above, or whitening only the expert down path while leaving the router alone.

comments.body: On lc1-b17-d768-bzl, we scaled the number of steps, so its not clear how much the ML changes happened. If we just consider the compute and the scaling law, what is the speedup of the ML changes. assume equal tps.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Re: [the question on `lc1-b17-d768-bzl`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5848255022). **The ML changes alone are worth about 1.10× compute at d768** (range 1.10–1.11×). At d512 they're worth about 1.11× (range 1.10–1.12×). This counts only the model/optimizer changes and gives no credit for throughput.

**Method.** I fit the clean-KMA ladder (d512 through d1280, each at its reference budget) to `L(C) = 1.2 + A·C^(−α)`, with L∞ = 1.2 as in the objective. The fit gives α = 0.0865, with residuals within ±0.009. For a candidate run, the effective compute multiplier over the baseline *at the same rung* is `((L_base − 1.2) / (L_run − 1.2))^(1/α)`. I anchor on the actual baseline run at that rung rather than the fitted curve, because the d768 baseline sits 0.009 below the fit. Dividing that multiplier by the compute the run actually used removes the extra steps. What remains is the ML-only speedup at equal tokens per second.

| rung | baseline loss | bzl loss | bzl compute / baseline | total effective multiplier | **ML-only (equal tps)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 2.8234 (2 runs) | 2.8016 | 1.057× (7324 vs 6928 steps) | 1.17× (1.16–1.18) | **1.10× (1.10–1.11)** |
| d512 | 3.1223 (2 seeds) | 3.0834 | 1.138× (2817 vs 2475 steps) | 1.27× (1.25–1.28) | **1.11× (1.10–1.12)** |

The ranges come from α: the local d512→d768 slope is 0.0913, the global fit 0.0865, and the local d768→d1024 slope 0.0840.

**Caveats**
- **Noise:** the noise level (about 0.005 of loss) corresponds to about ±3.5% compute at d768. The d768 figure rests on one bzl run.
- **Extra steps:** crediting them through the across-rung law assumes the rungs are near compute-optimal. There, a small extra amount of data alone buys about the same as extra compute along the frontier.
- **Throughput:** the extra steps come from throughput work: the fp32 embedding-gather backward (+12% ex/s) and, going forward, the MFU fixes (+5.5%). That is where the rest of the total 1.17–1.27× comes from.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 28: q/k sharpness, V-gate heatmaps, Delta AttnRes, multi-head AttnRes at d768** (branch `ladderclimb_v1_batch14`)

This batch follows up [the qk_mult comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5848415944) and [the multi-head / Delta AttnRes comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5849538511).

**Step-count rule, adopted.** ML changes validated at d768–d1280 now use the baseline's step counts (d768 6928, d1024 9268, d1280 16667). I restarted gate 2 on that basis as `lc1-g2-d1024-bs` (9268 steps) and `lc1-g2-d1280-bs` (16667 steps), with checkpointing. The earlier attempts used throughput-scaled counts. MFU changes are measured separately in ex/s.

**Why qk_mult grows.** MuonH's hyperball step keeps each matrix at its initial Frobenius norm for the whole run. |W_q| and |W_uk| (|W_k| on KDA) never change, so the only way the model can sharpen q·k is the free scalar. The new `muon_free` group keeps MuonH's step size, `−lr·|W₀|·d/|d|` (`d` = the Newton–Schulz direction), but drops the re-projection and adds decoupled weight decay `−lr·wd·W`. With roughly orthogonal steps, the norm settles near `|W|²/|W₀|² ≈ lr/(2·wd)`. At d512 (lr 0.0214) the sweep `wd ∈ {0, 0.001, 0.003, 0.01}` spans an unbounded norm, about 3.3×, about 1.9× and about 1× the initial norm. It applies to `attn_q` and `attn_k` on both KDA and MLA. Learnable qk_mult stays on, so we can watch whether it stops growing. The best WD from d512 then goes to d768.

**Can the learnable KV-latent RMSNorm cover this?** Not cleanly, and your guess is right. On the MLA layers, K and V both come from `kv_latent_norm(x·W_dkv)`, so raising its gain scales K and V together. Sharper logits would therefore also scale the attention output relative to the other AttnRes sources, and that output gets no RMSNorm before the AttnRes mix. The gain is also elementwise and on Adam, so it could learn it in principle, but it has to trade logit sharpness against V magnitude. Q is full-rank and not normalized, and it is also held fixed by the hyperball. The KDA layers L2-normalize q and k, so there the scale is fixed by construction (× 1/√128).

**Delta Attention Residuals (arXiv 2605.18855).** Their sources are the per-sublayer outputs `v_i = h_{i+1} − h_i`. Those are exactly the sources our full AttnRes already uses (embedding + each attention and MoE output). Their "AttnRes" baseline attends over *cumulative* states, which is where I think the misunderstanding you mentioned comes in. The real change is **additive routing**: `input = h̄ + Σ softmax(w·RMSNorm(v_i))·v_i`, where `h̄` is the plain residual stream, with no final gate. I implemented it as `attn_res_additive` (plus `attn_res_final_mode=sum`):
- **Delta AttnRes:** full AttnRes + additive.
- **Delta Block:** our block AttnRes + additive. At d512 every layer is a block.

**V-gate heatmaps.** `attn_res_v_gate` under full AttnRes now applies to the **KDA layers only**, and the V gates' source weights are logged (`train/attn_res/w_g{2L+i}_*`). That lets me plot what V attends to next to what the Q/K gate reads.

**Multi-head AttnRes at d768** (6928 steps, paired against a d768 recipe baseline at the same steps):
- 4 heads
- 4 heads with the query LR at ×3 and ×1/3 (`attn_res_query_lr_scale` 0.3 / 0.03, default 0.1)
- 4 heads with a learnable **temperature** per gate and head, init 1. It is redundant with the query's norm, so it only changes the optimization dynamics.
- 4 heads with **per-head RMSNorm** for the key norm, instead of one RMS over all 512 channels

`d768-fixqk` isolates learnable qk_mult at d768: the same recipe with qk_mult fixed at 2.5.

The d768 rows pair with `lc1-b28-d768-base`; the clean KMA baseline is 2.8234. Once the Delta AttnRes heatmap is in, I'll pick the next step you suggested: add the deltas as extra inputs over the combined space, or add a selective delta such as current vs most recent.


**Interim: q/k without hyperball.**
- **Diagnosis confirmed.** qk_mult now stays at about 2.42, against 4.1 / 3.8 on the two MLA layers with the hyperball. Instead, the q/k Frobenius norms grow about 3× (≈11 → ≈35 per layer).
- **But it loses:** wd 0 gives +0.0082, and wd 0.001 gives +0.0102. At wd 0.001 the norms barely differ from wd 0, so the gradients are far more aligned than the orthogonal-step estimate assumed.
- **Likely confound: KDA.** KDA L2-normalizes q and k, so their scale does nothing there. A growing norm only shrinks the relative step size, cutting the effective LR on KDA q/k by about 3×.
- **Follow-up:** `mla_qk` applies `muon_free` to the softmax layers' `w_q` and `w_uk` only, which is where the logit scale actually matters.

**V gate vs Q/K gate on the KDA layers** (`lc1-b28-fullv`, full AttnRes, final step; −0.0020 vs full AttnRes, neutral).

![V vs QK gate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/0339519553e09aff8da67d0c55a7869fe685dbad/v1/attnres_vgate_lc1-b28-fullv.png)

V does read the history differently, and heavier on the embedding, as you guessed. At **L4, V puts 0.32 on the embedding against 0.02 for Q/K**. V also skips attention outputs almost entirely: the L0–L3 attention outputs get ≤ 0.01 each from L4's V. It reads the MoE outputs instead, L0 MoE 0.21, L1 0.18 and L3 0.18. Q/K concentrates on the latest MoE outputs, L2 MoE 0.31 and L3 MoE 0.28. L1 and L2 look alike for both, mostly the previous MoE output. The split pays off only at the deepest KDA layer, which fits a loss change within noise at d512.

**Delta AttnRes as specified** (`lc1-b28-delta`: full AttnRes sources, additive routing, no final gate): **+0.0289 vs full AttnRes**, and +0.0230 vs block AttnRes.

![Delta AttnRes heatmap](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/0339519553e09aff8da67d0c55a7869fe685dbad/v1/attnres_full_lc1-b28-delta.png)

The paper's sharpness claim holds here. The max mean weight per gate is 1.0 / 1.0 / 0.97 / 0.86 / 0.97 / 0.76 / 0.55 / 0.71 / 0.88 / 0.28 / 0.36 / 0.28, against 1 / 0.83 / 0.82 / 0.47 / 0.66 / 0.39 / 0.36 / 0.31 / 0.33 / 0.20 / 0.21 / 0.18 for full AttnRes ([baseline heatmap](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/0339519553e09aff8da67d0c55a7869fe685dbad/v1/attnres_full_lc1-b18-full-fair.png)).

But what it learns is almost always **"add another copy of the most recent sublayer output"**: the diagonal is 0.97–1.0 up to L4, so each input is roughly `h̄ + v_{i−1}`. That amounts to a learned up-weighting of the latest output, and the rest of the stream stays at weight 1 throughout. Additive routing can only add. It cannot suppress a source, and replacement AttnRes relies on suppression here. For example, full AttnRes drives the embedding to ≤ 0.03 in most gates, and it gives the V gate its own profile. I read the +0.029 as the cost of losing that suppression. The paper's gains are over their cumulative-state AttnRes, whose sources are the running sums `h_i`, and those collapse to uniform. Our sources are already the per-sublayer outputs, so that collapse doesn't happen.

**Next, based on the heatmap.** The delta gate's one strong preference is the most recent output. Since our sources are already deltas, "combined space" here means giving the replacement gates the *cumulative* view as extra sources:
- **(a)** Full AttnRes plus the current plain residual `h̄` as one extra source per gate. The gate can then select "standard residual" as an option, alongside suppression.
- **(b)** Full AttnRes plus the recent cumulative states `h_{i−1}` and `h_{i−2}`, the selective version.

(a) is queued as `lc1-b28-fullstream`.

**q/k hyperball verdict.**
- **All q/k without the hyperball:** it loses at every weight decay (+0.0075 to +0.0102). This comes from the KDA layers, whose q and k are L2-normalized.
- **MLA q/k only:** neutral at both wd 0 (+0.0019) and wd 0.01 (+0.0020).
- **Reading:** on the MLA layers, the grown q/k norms (≈2.5–3× the initial ones) take over the job qk_mult was doing, and qk_mult stays at about 2.4 instead of growing to about 4. The two ways of sharpening come out equivalent. So qk_mult's growth was compensation for the hyperball pinning the norms, not a missing capability.
- **Next:** removing the hyperball buys nothing at d512, so I'm not spending d768 compute on it. The d768 \`fixqk\` run still measures what learnable qk_mult is worth at scale.

**d768 restart (22:55 UTC).** Kueue pre-empted all six d768 runs at steps 4535–6283 of 6928. They're requeued as `lc1-b28-d768-*-r`, with the same configs and steps and no checkpointing; the table links above point to the new runs.

**d768 readout (6928 steps, the baseline's step count).**
- **The recipe itself:** **2.8114 vs clean KMA's 2.8234 (−0.0120)** at equal steps, from the ML changes alone. That matches gate 2 at d1024 (−0.0116).
- **Multi-head AttnRes does not carry to d768.** Every variant lands within ±0.0011 of the recipe:
  - 4 heads: +0.0005
  - query LR ×3: +0.0001
  - query LR ×1/3: +0.0009
  - learnable temperature: −0.0011
  - per-head RMSNorm: −0.0002

  The −0.0027 at d512 was noise, or it fades with width. With the multi-head path's small throughput cost, it isn't worth adding to the recipe.
- **Learnable qk_mult at d768:** turning it off costs **+0.0024** (2.8138), below the noise level. Most of the qk_mult benefit is the fixed 2.5 multiplier. Learning it per layer adds at most a little, which fits the hyperball analysis: at d512 it was only compensating for the pinned q/k norms.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 29: output-delta AttnRes and hierarchical multi-head AttnRes** (replying to [the Delta AttnRes follow-up](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5850304033))

**Is Delta AttnRes a new method?** Mostly not. Your read is right: it's a misreading of AttnRes followed by a re-implementation of it. There is one real difference.
- **What the paper calls "AttnRes":** it attends over the *cumulative* states `h_i`, which is not what Kimi's AttnRes, or ours, does. That baseline collapses to near-uniform routing because consecutive `h_i` are nearly identical.
- **What they call deltas:** the sublayer outputs `v_i`, which are exactly the sources real AttnRes already uses.
- **The one addition:** additive routing, `h̄ + Σ α_i v_i`. On our model it loses: +0.0289 for full AttnRes and +0.0158 for block AttnRes. It learns to add one more copy of the most recent output, and additive routing can't suppress anything.

**An actual delta version.** `attn_res_source_delta` makes the sources consecutive differences of the gate's source sequence, `[embedding, v_0 − embedding, v_1 − v_0, …]`: the delta of the outputs. The logits score the deltas. It runs on top of full AttnRes, with the final gate as a plain sum (the final gate has no delta view), so it pairs with full AttnRes (3.0774). One thing to note: the deltas telescope, so a uniform mix over N deltas equals `v_last / N`. At init this reads mostly the latest output, unlike the uniform mix over outputs.

**Hierarchical multi-head AttnRes** (`attn_res_head_sub`, 4 heads).
- **Global query:** each gate keeps one full-width query `q`, which sets each source's overall strength.
- **Per-head correction:** head *h* adds a zero-init sub-query `s_h`, so its logit for source *n* is `q · k̂_n + s_h · k̂_n[slice h]` (**slice**: `s_h` is 128 wide and dots its own portion) or `q · k̂_n + s_h · k̂_n` (**full**: `s_h` is 512 wide and dots the whole key).
- **Mixing:** each head mixes its own 128-channel slice with its own softmax. `k̂` is RMS-normalized over all 512 channels.
- **How it's built:** both reduce to full-width effective per-head queries `q + s_h` (the slice version pads `s_h` with zeros outside its slice), so they share one scoring path.
- **How it differs:** the full version has the same expressivity as 4 independent full-width queries, but the global/sub split changes the optimization. Plain multi-head (`lc1-b24-arh4`, −0.0027) instead splits one query into 4 slice queries, with no shared global term.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| output-delta sources (full AttnRes, final gate = sum) | [`121d343ec0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/121d343ec0) | [lc1-b29-outdelta](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b29-outdelta) | 2712 | 723 | 3.4509 | 3.1473 | +0.0699 vs 3.0774 |
| hierarchical 4-head AttnRes, slice sub-queries (128 wide) | [`121d343ec0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/121d343ec0) | [lc1-b29-arh4-sub-slice](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b29-arh4-sub-slice) | 2817 | 796 | 3.3746 | 3.0850 | +0.0017 vs 3.0833 |
| hierarchical 4-head AttnRes, full-width sub-queries (512 wide) | [`121d343ec0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/121d343ec0) | [lc1-b29-arh4-sub-full](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b29-arh4-sub-full) | 2817 | 790 | 3.3707 | 3.0826 | −0.0007 vs 3.0833 |

The d768 multi-head runs from batch 28 are in flight: 4 heads, query LR ×3 / ×1/3, temperature and per-head RMSNorm, with the d768 baseline at 6928 steps. I'll run the hierarchical version at d768 if it beats plain 4-head at d512.

**Output-delta AttnRes: +0.0699 vs full AttnRes. It fails, as you expected.** Differencing consecutive outputs destroys what the gate relies on: each sublayer's own contribution. A delta source mixes two layers' outputs with opposite signs, and a uniform mix over deltas telescopes to `v_last / N`. So the gate starts out reading mostly the latest output and has to re-learn sums of deltas just to get back to one output.

**Also from batch 28: full AttnRes plus the plain residual `h̄` as one extra selectable source** (`lc1-b28-fullstream-r`) is neutral, **+0.0015**. Giving the gates a standard-residual option adds nothing, so the replacement gates already express what they need.

Runs now go to **cw-rno2a**, which has spare H100s and reads the same bucket. cw-us-east-02a is fully allocated to a 152-GPU production job plus about 300 GPUs of queued interactive evals. Gate 2 stays on 02a, mid-run.

**Hierarchical multi-head: neutral.**
- **Slice sub-queries:** +0.0017.
- **Full-width sub-queries:** −0.0007.

Both are within noise and no better than plain 4-head (−0.0027, one seed). Adding a shared global query over the per-head ones doesn't help at d512. The d768 multi-head runs will decide whether any multi-head AttnRes carries to scale. They are 4 heads, query LR ×3 / ×1/3, temperature and per-head RMSNorm, all at 6928 steps.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **MFU pass 2: Python GC pauses were costing 20–30% of wall-clock step time at d512/d768. Fixed in `e4c47ad1b0`.**

**Symptom.** Across the ladder runs, the mean step time was well above the median. About 6% of steps took 2–9× the median:

| run | median | mean | mean/median |
|---|---|---|---|
| clean KMA d768 | 443 ms | 508 ms | 1.146 |
| recipe d768 (`lc1-b28-d768-base-r`) | 405 | 469 | 1.157 |
| recipe d512 (`lc1-mfu1`) | 164 | 214 | 1.304 |
| d1024 (`lc1-g2-d1024-bs`) | 1511 | 1546 | 1.023 |

**What the d768 profile showed.** In the slow steps, rank 0 waits up to 1.3 s inside an all-gather while its own compute is unchanged. Another rank is late to the collective.

**Diagnosis.** Every rank logged its host gaps and GC pauses (`lc1-stall-diag`, 400 steps at d512). Every rank took **gen-2 GC pauses of 0.40–0.57 s**, about once every 27 steps, each at a different step. Each collective waits for whichever rank is paused. A full collection traverses every live Python object, including the model/optimizer pytrees and the compiled executables.

**Fix.** Before the loop: `gc.collect(); gc.freeze(); gc.disable()`. After a step completes, every `GC_EVERY_STEPS = 50` steps, every rank runs `gc.collect(); gc.freeze()` at the same step. GC is re-enabled after the loop.

| d512, 400 steps | median | mean | mean/median | steps > 1.5× median |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before (`lc1-stall-diag`) | 160.6 ms | 213.8 ms | 1.331 | 11.1% |
| `gc.freeze()` only (`lc1-stall-diag2`) | 160.0 | 183.0 | 1.144 | 16.8% |
| **freeze + disable + synchronized collect (`lc1-stall-diag3`)** | 160.3 | **161.7** | **1.008** | **0.0%** |

**Result.** Mean step time drops **24% (213.8 → 161.7 ms), about 1.32× wall-clock throughput at d512**. At d768 the expected gain is about 1.15×, from the observed mean/median ratio.

**Accounting caveat.** The ladder's step counts come from ex/s, and I've been using run *medians*, which never saw these stalls. So this doesn't change the fixed-time step counts under the current accounting, but it does cut real train-step time. The clean-KMA baselines carried the same stalls, so the "8 minutes" had really been 9–10 minutes of wall clock at d512. If train-step time should mean the *sum* of step durations, this fix alone is +32% steps at d512. **Do you want the step-count rule to switch from median to mean ex/s?**

- **Hash routing on layer 0: neutral (+0.0004).** A fixed token-id hash does as well as the learned router at L0, so L0 routing can be free.
- **Gumbel sampling:** neutral at τ 0.1 / 0.3 (+0.0031 / +0.0011) and harmful at τ 1.0 (+0.026). Stochastic expert choice buys nothing on top of QB.

**QK-norm replicates at d512:** seed 0 −0.0057 and seed 1 −0.0166 (vs a seed-1 recipe run at 3.0951), **mean paired −0.0112**. The d768 check (6928 steps, vs 2.8114) is running.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 31: weight EMA over the final steps, a raised final LR, and the EMA/final blend** (for [the EMA comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5852207930) and the blend follow-up; d512, vs `lc1-mfu1`, 3.0833)

**What's new** (`61fd676d50`):
- **`--ema-beta β --ema-last-steps n`:** the EMA follows the params until step `T − n`, then updates as `ema ← β·ema + (1−β)·params`. Evals after the EMA start score the EMA. It's one extra fp32 copy of the params, cheap at d512.
- **`--ema-blend a`** (repeatable): after training, the final eval also scores `a·EMA + (1−a)·final` for each `a`, logged as `eval_blend<a>/…`. One run sweeps the blend: `a = 0` is the raw final weights (a sanity check against the main eval) and `a = 1` is the pure EMA.
- **Final LR:** `--opt-set min_lr_ratio` (default 0.05) sets where the linear decay ends. The `lr30` control shows what raising it costs without an EMA.

**Grid.** β ∈ {0.95, 0.99, 0.995}; window n ∈ {200, 500, 1000} (the EMA's effective horizon is 20, 100 and 200 steps); final LR ratio ∈ {0.05, 0.15, 0.3}. Each run's final eval covers blends a ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}.

**Per-group next.** The winner will guide the per-group version: different β, cooldowns and blends per parameter group, e.g. the lm_head still cooling down to 0.05. That needs per-group `min_lr_ratio` and per-group blend evals, which I'll add once the global picture is clear.

Blend-sweep results will go below as each run finishes.

**Blend sweep, \`lc1-b31-e99-500\`** (β 0.99, last 500 steps, final LR 0.05). Rows are \`a·EMA + (1−a)·final\`:

| Paloma macro | 3.0844 | 3.0810 | 3.0790 | **3.0788** | 3.0799 |

The raw final weights match the recipe within noise (3.0844 vs 3.0833). The EMA helps even at the normal 0.05 floor, and the best blend (0.5–0.75) is −0.0056 against its own final weights, −0.0045 against the recipe.


**Final LR 0.3 + EMA: the EMA recovers most of the damage, but it doesn't beat the normal decay.**

| run | a=0 (raw) | 0.25 | 0.5 | 0.75 | 1 (EMA) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| β 0.99, last 500, LR 0.3 | 3.1841 | 3.1506 | 3.1289 | 3.1177 | **3.1163** |
| β 0.995, last 1000, LR 0.3 | 3.1834 | 3.1434 | 3.1192 | **3.1083** | 3.1086 |
| β 0.95, last 200, LR 0.3 | 3.1836 | 3.1680 | 3.1569 | 3.1505 | **3.1486** |

At 2817 steps, the cooldown to 0.05 is worth more than any EMA can recover from a 0.3 floor. The best is 3.1083, still +0.025 against the recipe. The one EMA that helps runs on top of the normal decay: β 0.99 / last 500 at LR 0.05 blends to −0.0045. Queued follow-ups at the 0.05 floor are longer windows and higher β (0.995 over the last 1000, 0.998 over the last 1500), plus one mild 0.1 floor with β 0.995. Per-group variants, such as a different β or cooldown for the lm_head, come once the global best is clear.

**EMA at the normal 0.05 floor: blending works.**

| run | a=0 (raw) | 0.25 | 0.5 | 0.75 | 1 (EMA) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| β 0.99, last 500 | 3.0844 | 3.0810 | 3.0790 | **3.0788** | 3.0799 |
| β 0.995, last 1000 | 3.0828 | 3.0775 | **3.0750** | **3.0750** | 3.0774 |
| β 0.998, last 1500 | 3.0841 | **3.0770** | **3.0770** | 3.0826 | 3.0923 |

**Best: β 0.995 over the last 1000 steps, 50/50 blend with the final weights: 3.0750, −0.0083 vs the recipe.** A higher β needs a smaller blend (β 0.998 peaks at 0.25–0.5), and the pure EMA gets worse as the window grows. A 0.1 floor + EMA is still running. A higher floor loses everywhere: 0.3 gives +0.025 or worse, and 0.15 gives +0.002. Next are the per-group variants (a separate β / blend for the lm_head, embeddings and matrices) around β 0.995 / last 1000, and a seed replicate of the best.

**Per-group probe** (`--ema-group-sweep`, commit `17e8e301a4`): every group starts at the 0.5 blend, then each group of {lm_head, embed, attn, moe, other} is set in turn to 0 (raw final) and 1 (pure EMA). The result is logged as `eval_blend_<group><a>/`. This shows which parameter groups want more or less averaging. Also: the 0.1 floor + EMA gives −0.0055 at best, worse than the 0.05 floor's −0.0083.

**EMA seed replicate** (β 0.995 / last 1000, seed 1): raw 3.0925, 50/50 blend 3.0849. The blend gains **−0.0076 over its own final weights**, against −0.0078 at seed 0, and is −0.0102 vs the seed-1 recipe. It is consistent: about −0.008 at no training cost.

**Per-group probe** (\`lc1-b33-emagrp\`). Every group starts at a 0.5 blend (3.0775), then one group at a time is set to its raw final weights or to its pure EMA:

| group | raw (a=0) | pure EMA (a=1) |
|---|---|---|
| attention | +0.0019 | 0.0000 |
| lm_head | +0.0021 | +0.0003 |
| **MoE / experts** | **+0.0041** | +0.0023 |
| embedding | +0.0001 | 0.0000 |
| other (norms, gates, AttnRes queries) | +0.0007 | −0.0001 |

- **MoE** gains the most from averaging, but wants a middle blend. Its pure EMA hurts, possibly because an averaged router falls out of step with the QB bias.
- **Attention and the lm_head** want ≥ 0.5.
- **Embedding and other** don't care.

A single global 0.5–0.75 blend is within about 0.001 of the best per-group choice, so per-group EMA isn't worth the extra machinery. **Recommendation:** β 0.995 over the last 1000 steps with a 0.5 blend, on top of the normal 0.05 floor. I'll combine it with the soft-cap next.

🤖 **Batch 32: zero-cost ideas from a literature scan** (d512, vs `lc1-mfu1`, 3.0833)

I scanned 2025–26 papers and the modded-nanogpt speedrun records for cheap ideas not already tried here. This batch takes the ones that cost nothing to run:
- **lm_head logit soft-cap** `c·tanh(z/c)`, c ∈ {15, 30} (Gemma 2; the tanh and asymmetric soft-cap speedrun records). The z-loss stays at 1e-4 per your rule, and eval scores the capped logits. The asymmetric `A·σ((z+B)/C)` form needs a kernel change, so it comes later if tanh helps.
- **Polar Express Newton–Schulz coefficients** (Amsel et al. 2025, arXiv 2505.16932): per-iteration minimax coefficients in MuonH, same 5 steps. Speedrun gain was about −0.002.
- **Negative-eigenvalue β in KDA** (Grazzi et al., ICLR 2025): `β = 2σ(logit − log 3)` ∈ (0, 2), so `I − βkkᵀ` can reflect. The mean β at init stays at 1/2.
- **LR floor 0** (Straight to Zero, Bergsma et al. 2025): linear decay all the way to 0, the opposite direction to batch 31's raised floor.

Next from the scan, in order:
1. Cautious weight decay on the Adam groups
2. A prefix-token auxiliary target (speedrun #88)
3. Gated DeltaNet-2's channel-wise erase gate in KDA (arXiv 2605.22791; needs a kernel change)
4. Default MoE's dense router gradient (arXiv 2504.12463)

**Readout: the three wins stack.**

| run | raw final | 0.5 blend | 0.75 blend |
|---|---|---|---|
| soft-cap 10 + EMA | 3.0617 | 3.0536 | **3.0531 (−0.0302)** |
| soft-cap 10 + QK-norm + EMA | 3.0572 | 3.0490 | **3.0486 (−0.0347)** |

The EMA blend adds its usual −0.008 over each run's final weights, and QK-norm adds −0.0045 on top of the cap. The full stack is **−0.035 at d512**. At d768, soft-cap 15 alone already gives −0.0157 (2.7957); cap 10 at d768 is running. The full stack at d768 is queued, with the EMA window scaled to the same 35.5% of training. If it holds, it becomes the gate-2 candidate at the baseline step counts (d1024 9268, d1280 16667).

**QK-norm dropped** (per your comment: it doesn't work with MLA, because normalizing q/k breaks the absorbed `W_uk` at inference). The candidate is now **soft-cap 10 + the EMA blend**: −0.0302 at d512. The d768 run is resubmitted without QK-norm as `lc1-b34-d768-cap10-ema`.

**d768: soft-cap 10 + EMA blend** (\`lc1-b34-d768-cap10-ema\`, 6928 steps; EMA β 0.995 over the last 2460 steps):
- raw final 2.7929, which matches cap 10 alone (2.7924)

comments.body: Lets test variations of 'One newer wrinkle: the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash paper appears to change this. There, because running Adam on the new Engram parameters would substantially increase optimizer-state memory, they instead optimize the Engram embedding tables, token embedding, and prediction head using a momentum-based update followed by Sinkhorn balancing, which like Muon needs only a momentum buffer and empirically outperformed Adam.'

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 35: Sinkhorn-balanced momentum for the embedding and lm_head** (for [the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5852942893); d512, on top of the new base = recipe + **soft-cap 10**, `lc1-b32-cap10`, 3.0591)

**The update** (`d80bbc35d6`):
- The optimizer keeps one fp32 momentum buffer, `m ← β·m + g`, with a Nesterov look-ahead `g + β·m`.
- The direction is that momentum after `k` Sinkhorn passes. Each pass rescales every row to unit RMS, then every column. The result is a matrix whose token rows and output channels all move at the same rate.
- It stores only a momentum buffer, like Muon (Adam keeps two moments). SinkGD, Scetbon et al. 2025, is the same idea.

**Where it applies:**
- **Embedding** (`embed_group=sinkhorn`): the direction × the Adam LR, replacing Adam.
- **lm_head** (`lm_head_group=sinkhornh`): the direction with the same Frobenius hyperball step AdamH uses, at the MuonH LR, replacing AdamH.
- On CPU, the rows and columns of the direction come out at RMS 1.000 and the hyperball keeps the lm_head norm.

**Variations:** both groups, head only, embed only, 1 vs 5 Sinkhorn passes, LR ×0.5 / ×2, and momentum 0.9 vs 0.95.

**Readout: Sinkhorn momentum matches Adam/AdamH at half the optimizer state, but doesn't beat them here.**

- It stores one fp32 buffer instead of Adam's two, which is DeepSeek's stated motivation. That matters for big tables: for the 524k-row bigram table in batch 36, the second moment alone would be 1 GB at d512.
- **Plan:** keep Adam/AdamH as the default, and use \`embed_group=sinkhorn\` for the large embedding tables if memory becomes the constraint.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 36: extra embeddings, done properly** (for [the embeddings comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5853011856); d512, on top of soft-cap 10, `lc1-b32-cap10`, 3.0591)

**Why the earlier embedding runs looked dead:**
1. **Throughput, not modelling.** In batch 1 every extra table paid the bf16 embedding-gradient scatter, so value embeds lost 11–13% ex/s and the second embedding 7%. Under the fixed-time rule that meant fewer steps. After the fp32 fix (batch 2) they were roughly neutral *against the fp32-only baseline*. Value embeds were −0.019 / −0.021 and the second embedding −0.022 against the old baseline, while the fp32 fix alone was −0.018.
2. **The bigram table was tiny.** `second_embed_bigram` hashed (previous, current) into only **16,384 rows**, the vocab size. There are about 2.7e8 possible bigrams, so almost every row is a collision soup, and that run was +0.0097. nanogpt's bigram table is many times the vocab.
3. **Only one integration was tried.** The second table only entered as one more AttnRes source, never as the nanogpt per-layer input.

**New** (`3a30fe13fc`):
- **`embed2_rows`** sets the table size, independent of the vocab.
- **`second_embed_mode=input`** is the nanogpt form. The table row is RMS-normalized and added to *every sublayer's AttnRes input* as `h + λ_g·rms(h)·ê`, with a learned λ per gate (init 0.1). Scaling to the mix's RMS makes λ a relative weight, so it survives the sublayer's RMSNorm. The table trains with Adam, using the fp32 gradient path.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 39: modded-nanogpt techniques** (for [the modded-nanogpt comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5853082249); d512, on top of soft-cap 10, 3.0591)

I pulled exact forms from the papers (MUDD arXiv 2502.12170, DCMHA arXiv 2405.08553, XSA arXiv 2603.09078) and from modded-nanogpt HEAD `bc3a0c2` (`train_gpt.py`, `dc_triton_kernels.py`, PRs 191/253/259/264/306/315/317/342/344).

**What's running:**
- **Learnable XSA.** Modded's form (record #82, PR 264) is `y − tanh(α_{layer,head})·⟨y,v̂⟩v̂` with **α zero-init**, i.e. no XSA at init. Adam, no WD. Their learned α: layer 7 ≈ +0.9, layer 8 ≈ 0.1–0.5. It's here as `xsa_mode=tanh`, next to the two earlier variants: `learned` (per-head scale, init 1 = today's full XSA) and `gated` (per-token `2σ(x·W)`, init 1).
- **DC attention on MLA** (`mla_head_mix`). Modded's lightweight DC (PR 315, one layer) is post-softmax, query-wise, rank-1: `y_h += w2_h(t)·Σ_s[Σ_g w1_g(t)·P_g(t,s)]·v_h(s)`, with a separate Triton kernel recomputing the scores. With per-head values that needs the probabilities, so a FlashAttention kernel can't provide it without changes. **The post-kernel variant here** is a per-token rank-1 mix of the head *outputs*: `y_h += w2_h(t)·Σ_g w1_g(t)·y_g`, with `w = x·W`, W2 zero-init, run after FA4 with no kernel change. With absorbed MLA, where all heads share the latent values, the two are exactly equivalent. With our per-head `W_uv` they differ, so this tests the cheap version first.
- **MUDD-style dynamic AttnRes** (`attn_res_dynamic_rank=64`). Our AttnRes is static-query MUDD with a softmax. MUDD's key delta is a **per-token dynamic** weight, `GELU(RMSNorm(X)·W1)·W2 + a`, with W2 zero-init and `a` = the static weights. Here each gate's softmax logits get `GELU(rms(stream)·W1)·W2` added: width 64, W1 ~ N(0, 1/D), W2 = 0, so it starts exactly at today's AttnRes. The paper's Table 5 puts most of the dynamic gain in the V and R (residual) streams, and our separate attention/MoE/V gates already give the multiway split.
- **Smear** (record #34): `x_t += λ·σ(x_t[:12]·w)·x_{t−1}` on the embedding, within documents, with λ init 0.

**Not planned:**
- **Paired-head attention** (#58) interleaves each head pair's q/k/v along the sequence. In MLA all heads share one latent key, so the trick degenerates. The workable equivalent (two latent KV tokens per position) doubles global-attention cost, which rules it out per your constraint.
- **FP8.** Modded's scheme is per-tensor `_scaled_mm`: weights quantised once per optimizer step in both layouts, delayed activation scales with 1.25 headroom, exact-current scales for output gradients, e4m3 for gradients, and FP8 on the lm_head and the MLP / QKV GEMMs. That's a throughput project, not a loss change, so I'm keeping it on the MFU list. On H100 it's per-tensor e4m3; on GB200 it would be MXFP8. It would need a per-expert scale for the MoE grouped GEMMs.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Lets see if you can come up with some crazy ideas here: think of model as animal that eats data. But it can't eat it immediately- instead it measures the gradient, and stores it in its lunchbox (optimizer state). Then it slowly consumes it over steps (based on optimizer momentum/beta). Usually model benefits from consuming that same data again later- because the copy it has in its lunchbox goes stale (gradient is no longer valid) and it didn't fully consume it the first time. Would be interesting if there was some gradient that could be measured that doesn't go stale so fast. Like, we want to compress and store the data in some 'natural state' that we can directly consume later. We have to space out when we consume the same data, so we dont get biased estimate of global grad. Just seems wasteful that we have to fwd/bwk pass on it again.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 42: data that doesn't go stale (the lunchbox idea)** (for [your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5853568170); d512, on top of soft-cap 10, 3.0591)

**Thinking it through.** A stored gradient `g(θ_t, x)` goes stale because it is tied to the parameters it was measured at: every factor in the chain rule (the activations in and the backpropagated error) is a function of θ_t. What we want to store is a piece of the computation that *doesn't* depend on the parameters we're still changing, or that depends on them only in a way we can recompute exactly and cheaply. Some options, ordered roughly from cheapest to hardest:

1. **Head replay: store the "view" instead of the gradient.**
   - For the lm_head, `∇W = Σ_t (softmax(W h_t) − y_t) h_tᵀ`. If we store the final hidden states `h_t` and labels `y_t` (not the gradient), the head's gradient on that data can be recomputed **exactly at the current W** for the cost of one head GEMM + CE (about 8% of a step), with no body forward/backward.
   - Only `h_t` is stale, as the body's view of the data at storage time. The head is also the part that sees each token's information most directly, and with a 16k vocab most rows see few tokens per step.
   - **Implemented** (`--head-replay SLOTS PERIOD SCALE`, `e9b58618db`). Every PERIOD steps the batch's `(h, y, weight)` goes into the next of SLOTS slots, and each step adds `SCALE·CE(W·stop_grad(h_old), y_old)` for the oldest slot. A stored batch is therefore consumed about (SLOTS−1)·PERIOD to SLOTS·PERIOD steps later, spaced out as you asked, and replayed PERIOD times at a small weight.
   - On CPU, only the lm_head gradient changes. Memory is about 67 MB per slot per GPU at d512.
2. **Top-k-layer replay.** The same idea one level deeper: store the inputs to the last k layers and replay only those layers + head. That costs k/L of a step, and the stored inputs go stale more slowly than a gradient does. With AttnRes, the "input" is the whole source history, so this is heavier, but it's the natural generalization if (1) works.
3. **Store local targets, not gradients** (target-propagation flavour). For a linear map, what stays useful is the pair (input, desired output): `∇W ½‖W x − t‖²` can be recomputed exactly at the current W. The target `t = W_old x − η·δ` bakes in one error signal, and the regression toward t can be re-consumed later. It goes stale as the upstream x and the downstream meaning of t drift, but more slowly than δ alone, because it keeps both sides. It's cheap per layer, and the tricky part is choosing η.
4. **Correct stale momentum instead of replaying.** STORM/SVRG-style: `m_t = g_t + β(m_{t−1} − g(θ_{t−1}; x_t))`. It needs a second gradient at the old parameters, so it costs roughly 2×. A Hessian-vector correction `m ← m + H(θ_t − θ_{t−1})` is cheaper, but it is still an extra backward. Probably a loss at our fixed time.
5. **Natural coordinates for sparse rows.** The embedding / bigram rows are touched rarely and have exact gradients (`∂L/∂e_v = Σ_{t: x_t = v} δ_t`) that stay valid as long as the layers above don't move much. A per-row accumulated signal consumed more slowly than Adam's β2 would work like an Adagrad-ish lunchbox. The Sinkhorn results suggest row balancing matters there.

I'm starting with (1), because it is exact for the head, cheap, and directly tests "consume old data without a forward/backward". The grid covers staleness (lag about 20–40, 100–200 and 750–1000 steps) and weight (0.1 / 0.3).

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| head replay, 2 slots × 100 steps (lag 100–200), scale 0.1 | [`11e2979fad`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/11e2979fad) | [lc1-b42-rp-2x100-s01](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b42-rp-2x100-s01) | 2817 | 738 | 3.3461 | 3.0664 | +0.0073 vs 3.0591 |
| head replay, 2 × 100, scale 0.3 | [`11e2979fad`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/11e2979fad) | [lc1-b42-rp-2x100-s03](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b42-rp-2x100-s03) | 2817 | 729 | 3.3779 | 3.0911 | +0.0320 vs 3.0591 |
| head replay, 2 × 20 (lag 20–40), scale 0.1 | [`11e2979fad`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/11e2979fad) | [lc1-b42-rp-2x20-s01](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b42-rp-2x20-s01) | 2817 | 725 | 3.3380 | 3.0642 | +0.0051 vs 3.0591 |

**Rerun (`11e2979fad`):** the first submissions hit NaN at step 2. Before a slot fills, its loss weights were all zero, so the replay's weighted-mean CE was 0/0 = NaN, and 0 × NaN stays NaN even at replay scale 0. Unfilled slots now carry unit weights; the rows above point to the reruns.

**Result: head replay hurts at every setting.** A higher replay weight hurts more (0.1 → +0.007, 0.3 → +0.032), and so does more staleness (lag 20–40 +0.005, lag 100–200 +0.007, lag 750–1000 +0.012), even at equal steps. Stale `h` is the problem. The head gets pulled toward an old body's view of the data, which fights the current body. The body moves too fast here for a stored view to stay useful. Option (2) would have the same problem one level deeper, so I'm not pursuing the replay line further. Options (3) and (5) remain untried.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 44: modded-nanogpt partial key offset + backout** (d512, on top of soft-cap 10; seed 0 vs 3.0591, seed 1 vs 3.0675; `1dc14be732`)

- **Partial key offset** (modded-nanogpt record #49, `mla_key_offset`). On the two MLA layers, the first half of each head's key channels are replaced with the *previous* token's key channels (zeroed at document starts). A query can then match "the token after X" in a single layer, which gives a one-layer induction head. It adds no parameters and has negligible cost. It is causal, which I checked on CPU: perturbing the last token leaves earlier outputs unchanged.
- **Backout** (modded-nanogpt's "backout" of the early residual, `attn_res_final_signed`). Our final AttnRes gate is a softmax over sources, so it can only *add* sources convexly. It cannot subtract, for example, the raw-embedding source from the lm_head input. This adds learned zero-init signed coefficients: `final = softmax_mix + Σ_n c_n·source_n`. That is 6 scalars, trained with Adam.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 45: SNOO outer loop + Default-MoE dense router gradient** (d512, on top of soft-cap 10, 3.0591; from the second literature pass)

- **SNOO** ([arXiv 2510.15830](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15830), `snoo_period`). Each group's normal optimizer (MuonH / AdamH / Adam) runs as the inner loop on the fast weights. Every K steps the slow weights take a Nesterov step on the pseudo-gradient `s = slow − fast` (`b ← μb + s`, `slow ← slow − η(μb + s)`), and the fast weights jump to them. The inner optimizer state is never reset.
  - The paper reports a 1.4–1.7× compute factor on dense models and 1.2–2.0× on MoE up to 1e23 FLOPs, growing with scale. I expect less over an 8-minute horizon.
  - Adaptations: hyperball leaves are projected back to their per-layer Frobenius norm after each outer step, because the extrapolation leaves the sphere. The QB `router_bias` is controller state and passes through. On CPU, the wrapper matches SGD at K=1/η=1/μ=0 and matches a hand calculation at K=2.
  - It costs two fp32 parameter-sized buffers. The sweep covers K ∈ {10, 20, 50}, η 0.5 → 0.8, and μ 0.5 → 0.25.
- **Dense router gradient** (Default MoE, [arXiv 2504.12463](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12463), `moe_dense_router_grad`). Top-k routing gives the router a gradient only for the 8 experts it picked. This adds `Σ_{e∉top-k} (w_e − sg(w_e))·sg(ȳ_e)`, where `w_e` is the renormalized sigmoid weight the expert would have had.
  - The term is zero in the forward pass; on CPU the loss is identical.
  - `ȳ_e` is expert e applied to the mean latent input of the tokens routed to it in this batch. The paper uses an EMA of the expert's outputs; this is a stateless stand-in, computed in the experts' EP sharding. On CPU it changes the router gradient by about 15% at init.

| SNOO K=10 | [`7dd3c91c37`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/7dd3c91c37) | [lc1-b45-snoo10](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b45-snoo10) | 2817 | 779 | 3.3308 | 3.0604 | +0.0013 vs 3.0591 |
| SNOO K=50 | [`7dd3c91c37`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/7dd3c91c37) | [lc1-b45-snoo50](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b45-snoo50) | 2817 | 778 | 3.3134 | 3.0649 | +0.0058 vs 3.0591 |
| SNOO K=20, η 0.8 | [`7dd3c91c37`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/7dd3c91c37) | [lc1-b45-snoo20-lr8](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b45-snoo20-lr8) | 2817 | 779 | 3.4064 | 3.0846 | +0.0255 vs 3.0591 |
| SNOO K=20, μ 0.25 | [`7dd3c91c37`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/7dd3c91c37) | [lc1-b45-snoo20-m25](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b45-snoo20-m25) | 2817 | 784 | 3.3115 | 3.0749 | +0.0158 vs 3.0591 |
| dense router gradient | [`7dd3c91c37`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/7dd3c91c37) | [lc1-b45-dense](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b45-dense) | 2817 | 776 | 3.3386 | 3.0586 | −0.0005 vs 3.0591 |
| dense router gradient, seed 1 | [`7dd3c91c37`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/7dd3c91c37) | [lc1-b45-dense-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b45-dense-s1) | 2817 | 782 | 3.3417 | 3.0617 | −0.0058 vs 3.0675 |

**SNOO, interim (3 of 5 finished): the mid-run gain doesn't survive the LR decay.**

| K | mid loss (base 3.3386) | final Δ |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 3.3308 (−0.008) | +0.0013 |
| 20 | 3.3219 (−0.017) | +0.0003 |
| 50 | 3.3134 (−0.025) | +0.0058 |

At mid-run, SNOO is ahead by 0.008–0.025, and a longer outer period gives a bigger lead. At the end of the schedule it is neutral to worse: the decay phase already delivers the averaging and extrapolation benefit that the outer Nesterov step gives mid-run. This matches the paper's gains growing with horizon; at our 8-minute horizon, the whole run is short relative to the decay. **Final: SNOO is out at this scale.**
- η 0.8 (at K=20): +0.0255; its mid-run loss was 3.4064, so the larger outer step already hurt mid-run.
- μ 0.25 (at K=20): +0.0158, though its mid-run loss was 3.3115.
- No SNOO setting beats the base at the end of the schedule.

**Dense router gradient: neutral to small.** It gives −0.0005 on seed 0 and −0.0058 on seed 1, a mean of −0.003, which is inside the 0.0056 seed noise, at unchanged ex/s (776 / 782). With 384 experts and QB balancing, the non-selected experts' routing seems to be learned well enough already. I'm not adding it to the stack.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 46: two Muon direction variants** (d512, on top of soft-cap 10, 3.0591; from the second literature pass)

Both change only the MuonH direction, before the Frobenius hyperball step, and add no memory.

- **MuonEq** ([arXiv 2603.28254](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28254), `muon_pre_norm`). Before Newton–Schulz, normalize the Nesterov momentum so each output unit's column (`out`) or each input unit's row (`in`) has unit norm. Newton–Schulz then orthogonalizes a pre-equilibrated matrix, so a few large rows can't dominate the polar factor. NorMuon, which was neutral here, normalizes *after* NS; this acts *before* it.
- **SAMuon-lite** ([arXiv 2608.25990](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25990), `muon_top_shrink`). SAMuon's update is `γ·NS(M) − (γ−1)·u₁v₁ᵀ`: amplify the spectral bulk and hold the top direction at 1. Because our hyperball step fixes the update's overall scale, that reduces to `NS(M) − (1 − 1/γ)·u₁v₁ᵀ`, i.e. removing a fraction of the top singular direction.
  - `(u₁, v₁)` comes from 3 stateless power iterations on the momentum, started from its column sums. It recovers the top pair on a CPU test.
  - The paper reports 13–24% fewer tokens than Muon at 124M–1B on modded-nanogpt variants. It ramps γ in over the first 30% of training; this version holds γ constant.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 47: three cheap literature items** (d512, on top of soft-cap 10; seed 0 vs 3.0591, seed 1 vs 3.0675)

- **SSMax on the two MLA layers** ([arXiv 2501.19399](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19399), `mla_ssmax`). The MLA layers are NoPE, so the attention logit scale doesn't know how many keys a query competes over. Each query is scaled by `1 + s_h·log(n)`, where n is the number of keys it can see in its own document and `s_h` is a zero-init per-head parameter trained with Adam. The model starts unchanged. The Inkling bias term is not scaled, and FA4 is untouched.
- **Canon-C** (Physics of LMs 4.1, [arXiv 2512.17351](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.17351), `sconv_sites=attn,mlp,mlp_in`). We already have short convs on the q/k/v projections (Canon-B) and on both branch outputs. This adds the identity-init causal depthwise conv on the *normed MoE input*, so the router and experts see a local token mix. Earlier, dropping the branch-output convs cost about +0.003 at d512, so local mixing helps some here.
- **Shared-expert sigmoid gate** (Qwen2-MoE / Qwen3-Next, `shared_expert_gate`). The shared experts' output is scaled per token by `2σ(x·w)`, with `w` zero-init so the gate starts at 1. That lets the model turn down the shared path on tokens where the routed experts carry the load.

All three are causal and get gradients on CPU.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 48: a truly ungated ReLU² expert kernel, and the stack on it** (d512, equal steps first, to measure ex/s)

The ReLU² expert wins (batches 41 and 43) so far paid for a *tied* gate: I passed `[W_up | W_up]` so that `relu(u)·u = relu(u)²`. That runs the up GEMM twice, which put those rows at 620–650 ex/s against 795. At fixed time, that cost more steps than the loss gain was worth.
- **Kernel change** (`6526a821da`): the pooled-wave EP backend treats a `w13` whose width equals the intermediate dim as ungated and computes `act(x·W_up)·W_down`. The model sends `W_up` alone with relu² when `moe_ungated_kernel=true`. The dropless sonic_cute eval backend keeps the tied form, which is the same math.
- **Check:** on a 4-device CPU EP mesh, the loss is bitwise identical and all gradients agree to 4e-7 relative.
- **Expected speed:** 576 experts / top-12 with a 2-GEMM expert has the same FLOPs as 384 / top-8 with a 3-GEMM SwiGLU. The dispatch moves 1.5× as many assignments, though, so I expect ex/s a bit under the base.
- **Plan:** these rows run at the base's 2817 steps to confirm they reproduce the tied runs' losses and to measure ex/s. The fixed-time runs follow with steps from that ex/s.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 49: Muon2 (Adam-preconditioned Muon)** (d512, on top of soft-cap 10, 3.0591)

This is [Muon2 (arXiv 2604.09967)](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.09967v2), `muon_precond_beta2`. MuonH keeps a bias-corrected EMA `v` of the squared gradient for each matrix leaf and runs Newton–Schulz on `M ⊘ (√v̂ + ε)` instead of on the momentum `M`. The step still goes through the hyperball.
- **How it differs from what we've tried:**
  - NorMuon (neutral here) normalizes per neuron *after* NS.
  - MuonEq (batch 46) normalizes whole rows or columns before NS.
  - This one is *elementwise* Adam preconditioning before NS.
- **Reported:** GPT-Base val PPL 21.47 → 20.39 with 3 NS steps; it beats NorMuon and AdaMuon and reaches Muon's loss in about 25% fewer steps.
- **Cost:** one fp32 buffer per MuonH matrix.

| Muon2, β₂ 0.99 | [`a81a220ac9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a81a220ac9) | [lc1-b49-muon2-99](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b49-muon2-99) | 2817 | | | queued | vs 3.0591 |

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: on partial key offset, make sure its still compatible with inference time MLA absorption.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **On partial key offset and MLA absorption:** it stays compatible. The KV cache is unchanged, and only the absorbed QK product widens.

- **Our MLA key:** per head h, the key is `k_{j,h} = W_uk,h · c_j`, with `c_j = RMSNorm(x_j W_dkv)` the cached latent. (The k-side short conv is off in this config: `sconv_sites=attn,mlp`.)
- **The offset** takes the first half of each head's key channels from the previous token: `k_{j,h} = [W_uk,h^A c_{j−1} ; W_uk,h^B c_j]`, where A/B are the first and second halves of W_uk,h's output columns, and the A half is zeroed at a document start.
- **The score still absorbs**, now into two latent-space queries:
  `q_h · k_{j,h} = (W_uk,h^Aᵀ q_h^A) · c_{j−1} + (W_uk,h^Bᵀ q_h^B) · c_j = q̃^A_h · c_{j−1} + q̃^B_h · c_j`.
- **What it costs at inference:**
  - The cache still stores only `c_j`. `c_{j−1}` is the previous row of the same cache, so it needs no extra storage, and in a tiled kernel it is one extra row per KV tile.
  - The QK dot is over 2 × kv_latent instead of kv_latent. Equivalently, the kernel treats the cache as `[c_{j−1} ; c_j]` against `[q̃^A ; q̃^B]`.
  - The document-start mask zeroes the `c_{j−1}` term for the first key of each document; for a single-document decode, that is just j = 0.
  - Values and the W_uv absorption are unchanged.
- **Other terms:** the Inkling relative bias, qk_mult and SSMax (if kept) act on q or on the logits, not on the cached latent, so they don't interact with this.
- **Results so far:** −0.0061 / −0.0116 on two seeds at d512 (batch 44). It is in the stacked run in batch 48.
